docs.title: Nephilex
docs.text:
Find vulnerabilities, see how untrusted input reaches them, and apply fixes that Nephilex re-checks before it commits them.

Nephilex is an open-source (Apache-2.0) application security scanner for the command line. One nephilex scan covers source code, dependencies, secrets, infrastructure as code, CI workflows, containers and LLM/agent configuration, and produces one prioritized list. It runs offline by default and needs no API key; the dependency scanner sends package names and versions to OSV to look up advisories.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Python 3.10 or newer. The [ast] extra installs the tree-sitter parsers the data-flow (taint) scanners need; without it those scanners are skipped.

pipxpip 
pipx install "nephilex[ast]"

python -m pip install "nephilex[ast]"

Scan the deliberately vulnerable demo app from the repository:

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/nephilex/nephilex.git
nephilex scan nephilex/examples/vulnerable-app --no-ai

    Five minutes from install to an HTML report, a SARIF file, a CI gate and editor setup, with the expected output of every step.

  • Example finding

    One finding from the demo app followed end to end: the code, the report, the proposed patch, how it is verified and what the re-scan shows.

  • Trust and limits

    How accuracy is measured, what is static and what is live, a capability matrix per scanner, and where established tools are stronger.

    Precision and recall on a labeled corpus and on public datasets, scored next to Bandit and Semgrep, with the methodology and its caveats.

Status: early alpha (0.x)

The architecture and full pipeline are in place: a working CLI, built-in scanners (secrets, dependencies, SAST, IaC, CI/CD, containers, cloud, supply chain, LLM and agent configuration), a multi-provider AI layer, cross-file taint analysis, and nine report formats. Detection accuracy is still being benchmarked. Treat findings as a strong signal to review, not gospel.

docs.title: What Nephilex does
docs.text:
• Maps the project first. Detects languages and frameworks and records an architecture summary (APIs, auth, datastores, cloud, containers, CI/CD, dependency manifests) that the scanners and the risk score use.
  • Runs layered analysis in one pass. Secrets, dependency CVEs (OSV data, with optional import-level reachability), pattern SAST, tree-sitter taint analysis for Python and JavaScript/TypeScript, IaC misconfiguration, and an LLM/agent scanner mapped to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Apps.
  • Explains each finding. Why it is a vulnerability, how an attacker would use it, business impact, likelihood, severity, and a CWE/OWASP mapping.
  • Fixes what it can verify. For a small set of rules Nephilex has a deterministic one-line rewrite. It applies a rewrite only when the rule no longer matches the changed line and, for Python, JSON and YAML, the file still parses. nephilex fix commits the changes to a new branch and opens a pull request only when you pass --open-pr. Nothing is auto-merged.
  • Keeps your code on your machine. The default AI provider is offline. Ollama runs locally. Cloud models are opt-in.

docs.title: What Nephilex does not do
docs.text:
Security engineers trust tools that state their limits:

Static analysis first, not DAST

Nephilex reads code and configuration. With --live-target it also makes a few read-only GET requests to a URL you are authorized to test: whether the site uses HTTPS, security headers, cookie flags, version disclosure, a short list of exposed paths (such as /.env and /.git/config), wildcard CORS, and whether a harmless marker sent in the URL's existing query parameters is reflected. It does not crawl, fuzz endpoints, or test authenticated flows.

  • Taint depth varies by language. Data-flow analysis covers Python and JavaScript/TypeScript and needs the [ast] extra. Cross-file analysis is Python only and follows one call hop. Other languages get pattern rules, not data-flow analysis.
  • Fix verification is a local re-check unless you ask for tests. By default, "verified" means the rule no longer fires on the rewritten line and the file still parses; it does not prove the new code is correct. nephilex fix --verify-with-tests also runs your test suite in a temporary copy of the repository before and after the fixes and commits only fixes that keep it passing (see Fixing & pull requests). Neither runs the application itself; see the example finding for what that means in practice.
  • Not a full enterprise ASPM. No ticketing and no SSO. Policies (nephilex policy check, see Policy) gate a scan in CI; they are not organization-wide governance. It is a scanner and a fixer, not a platform.
  • Dependency coverage follows OSV. A vulnerability absent from OSV is absent from Nephilex. Without network access the scanner falls back to a small bundled advisory list and says so. Reachability lowers noise but is heuristic, not a proof.
  • Not a replacement for a human review or a pen test. A clean scan means "nothing these checks caught," not "secure."

The full list, scanner by scanner, is in Trust and limits.

docs.title: Server agent
docs.text:
The Nephilex server agent monitors one or more paths on a host on a schedule. It is the deployment-friendly form of continuous monitoring: run under systemd, in cron, or as a long-lived process.

For a single repository, nephilex watch is enough. Use the agent when you need to monitor multiple paths on a server (application code, config directories, etc.) with one config file.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
nephilex agent --init
# edit .nephilex/agent.yml, then:
nephilex agent --once
nephilex agent              # run until Ctrl+C

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
See examples/agent.yml:

interval: 600
state_dir: .nephilex/agent
push: true
cloud_url: ${NEPHILEX_CLOUD_URL}
cloud_token: ${NEPHILEX_CLOUD_TOKEN}
fail_on_drift: high
host_label: prod-web-01

targets:
  - path: /var/www/my-app
    scanners: secrets, patterns, sca, iac
  - path: /etc/nginx
    scanners: patterns

Each target is scanned every cycle. Snapshots and drift history are stored under state_dir (per target). When push is enabled, results are sent to Nephilex Cloud with the host label prefixed on the target name.

docs.title: systemd example
docs.text:
[Unit]
Description=Nephilex security agent
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=nephilex
WorkingDirectory=/opt/my-app
Environment=NEPHILEX_CLOUD_URL=https://cloud.example.com
Environment=NEPHILEX_CLOUD_TOKEN=...
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/nephilex agent --config /opt/my-app/.nephilex/agent.yml
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

docs.title: Cron example
docs.text: */15 * * * * /usr/local/bin/nephilex agent --config /opt/my-app/.nephilex/agent.yml --once -q

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Nephilex is built as a small, strict core with everything domain-specific pushed out to plugins. This document describes the core, the data flow, and where the seams are.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
A scan is a linear pipeline. Each stage has a single responsibility and passes a well-defined object to the next.

              targets.resolve
 target ───────────────────────▶ Project (or WebTarget)
                                    │
        RepositoryAnalyzer.analyze  │  languages, frameworks, architecture
                                    ▼
                             enriched Project
                                    │
             ScanEngine.scan        │  select applicable scanners
                                    ▼
                         [ Scanner.scan(ctx) ]*   ──▶  Finding[]
                                    │
              agents (per finding)  │  EnrichmentAgent -> AttackSimulationAgent -> PatchAgent
                                    ▼
                              ScanResult
                                    │
             Reporter.render        │  json | sarif | markdown | html | csv | badge | vex
                                    ▼
                             report string(s)

The engine (nephilex.core.engine.ScanEngine) owns orchestration. It is synchronous and never modifies scanned source: scan() returns a ScanResult. It writes in two places. The first is Nephilex's own scan-cache directory (disable with --no-cache / cache: false). The second is the project's .nephilex/audit.log: for a trusted local project, each suppression that hid or accepted a finding (allowlist entry, exception, inline nephilex-ignore comment) is appended once (disable with audit_log: false or NEPHILEX_AUDIT_LOG=off; see Audit log). Cloned remotes, --config-from-ref runs, nephilex agent and nephilex mcp never write to the scanned tree. The engine also leaves the caller's Project object alone: config such as exclude_paths and the analyzer's results are applied to a copy, so one Project can be scanned by several engines with different configs. ScanEngine.postprocess() runs the same post-scan steps on findings that came from elsewhere, such as imported SARIF. Writing reports and creating pull requests are separate, explicit actions performed by the CLI or an integration.

docs.title: Core modules
docs.text: Module Responsibility nephilex.core.models The Finding, ScanResult, Severity, Remediation, and ExploitScenario data types. Everything speaks these. nephilex.core.project Project and FileRef: a normalized, lazily-read view of the target. Scanners consume this, never the filesystem directly. nephilex.core.plugin The Scanner/Reporter contracts, ScannerContext, PLUGIN_API_VERSION and the global Registry. nephilex.plugin_api The public, versioned plugin surface: re-exports the names plugins may depend on. nephilex.core.config Config loading and defaults. nephilex.core.engine The ScanEngine orchestrator. nephilex.core.gitexec The only place Nephilex runs git; see Running git. nephilex.analysis.repository RepositoryAnalyzer: language, framework, and architecture detection. nephilex.ai The AIProvider contract and the heuristic/Anthropic/OpenAI/Ollama providers, plus the selection factory. nephilex.agents Finding-processing agents: enrichment, attack simulation, patch generation. nephilex.scanners Built-in scanners. nephilex.reporting Built-in reporters. nephilex.targets Resolves a target string into a Project or WebTarget. nephilex.context Loads and applies .nephilex/context.yml (sanitizers, trusted sources, internal paths, exposure, data classification); see Project context. nephilex.audit The hash-chained .nephilex/audit.log: event builders, append under a lock, verification and export; see Audit log. nephilex.importers SARIF 2.1.0 import into ordinary findings, and the merge with Nephilex's own; see Importing SARIF. nephilex.cli The Typer command-line interface; see The CLI package.

docs.title: The Finding contract
docs.text:
Finding is the load-bearing type. A scanner is responsible for identity, location, severity, and taxonomy (CWE/OWASP). The reasoning fields (why_vulnerable, attacker_perspective, business_impact), the ExploitScenario, and the Remediation.patch may be filled by the scanner or completed later by an agent. This split is what lets a simple regex scanner and a sophisticated AI agent contribute to the same finding without coupling.

risk_score() blends severity, confidence, and likelihood into a 0 to 100 number; ScanResult.aggregate_risk() rolls findings up into a single target score that is dominated by the worst finding rather than averaged.

docs.title: The CLI package
docs.text:
nephilex.cli is split so that a change to one command touches one file:

Module Contents cli/app.py Builds the Typer app: root callback and --version, the handler that turns any ConfigError into exit status 2, built-in plugin registration, then the built-in and third-party commands. cli/commands/ One module per command family: scan, check (check, the fast file-level check editors and AI hooks run), imports (import; the module name avoids the Python keyword), focused (secrets, iac, api, cicd, container, cloud, infrastructure), supply_chain (sbom, dependencies, supply-chain), inventory (inventory, drift), monitor (watch, agent, server), baseline, policy, audit (audit verify, audit show, audit export), remediate (fix, review, learn), service (push, dashboard, mcp) and meta (scanners, reporters, providers, version, init). cli/commands/__init__.py register_commands(app), the ordered list of built-in commands. Typer shows commands in nephilex --help in registration order, so new commands are added there. cli/app.py then adds import and the audit group after it. cli/_common.py Helpers the commands share: severity and list parsing, target resolution (exit 2 on failure), the progress printer, config assembly from flags, baseline and diff filtering, and the gate that fails a run when scanners crashed. cli/output.py Report emission through the reporter registry, the console table and posture panel, the fix summary, and verbatim stdout writes for machine-readable output. cli/_console.py The stdout and stderr Rich consoles, with UTF-8 forced on Windows. cli/plugins.py Loads nephilex.commands entry points through the plugin allowlist. cli/main.py The console-script target (nephilex.cli.main:app); it only re-exports app. cli/starter_config.yml The .nephilex.yml written by nephilex init.

Command functions are plain functions that take Typer options; they call into nephilex.core and the domain packages and keep presentation in output.py. Every command module is imported when the CLI starts (Typer needs the signatures), so anything heavy a command uses, such as Rich tables, report formats or an HTTP client, is imported inside the function that needs it. nephilex check runs after every edit in an editor hook and depends on this. Exit codes follow the CLI contract in COMPATIBILITY.md: 0 for a pass, 1 for findings at the --fail-on threshold or crashed scanners in a gating run, 2 for usage, target and configuration errors.

docs.title: Plugin discovery
docs.text:
Two registration paths feed the same global Registry:

  1. In-process, importing a scanner/reporter/provider module runs its @scanner/@reporter/@ai_provider decorator, registering the class. The built-ins use this via nephilex.plugins.register_builtins, which imports the scanners and defers the reporters and AI providers: the first lookup of either kind (registry.reporters(), registry.get_ai_provider(...)) imports them, so a command that never needs a report format or a model client does not pay for importing it. A built-in always keeps its name, even when a third-party plugin registered the same name first.
  2. Entry points, third-party packages declare a callable under the nephilex.plugins entry-point group in their pyproject.toml. The registry loads these lazily on first lookup. A failure in one plugin is isolated and never aborts discovery of the others.

Third-party code imports from nephilex.plugin_api, which re-exports the stable contract and PLUGIN_API_VERSION. Every Scanner, Reporter and AIProvider class carries an api_version; the registry skips a class whose version does not match, logs which plugin was skipped, and leaves the scan running without it. The separate nephilex.commands entry-point group lets packages add CLI subcommands; it is loaded by cli/plugins.py under the same allowlist.

See plugins.md for how to write one and for the stability rules.

docs.title: Running git
docs.text:
Every git invocation goes through nephilex.core.gitexec. It builds an argument list (never a shell), pins repository config keys that would make git launch a program (core.fsmonitor, diff.external, textconv, core.pager, signature display) with -c, adds --no-textconv/--no-ext-diff/--no-show-signature where the subcommand accepts them, disables terminal prompts, applies a timeout, caps stdout and decodes it with invalid bytes replaced, and provides is_safe_ref for refs that come from flags or config.

It has two profiles:

  • UNTRUSTED for reading a repository that is being scanned. On top of the shared pins it disables hooks, credential helpers, SSH and proxy commands, every transport (protocol.allow=never, no lazy fetch) and the system git config, and strips environment variables that could redirect git or inject helpers. nephilex.scanners._git (run_git, used by the git-security and history scanners), the dependency diff in nephilex.inventory, --config-from-ref in nephilex.core.config and the file walk in nephilex.core.project (which asks git for the untracked files it ignores) use it.
  • WORKTREE for the operator's own checkout, where nephilex fix and nephilex review create branches, commit and push. Hooks, commit signing and credentials stay available because those steps need them. nephilex.remediation.git_ops uses it.

Cloning a remote target is the one exception: nephilex.targets runs git clone itself with its own transport allowlist and hardening.

docs.title: AI providers and the offline default
docs.text: Agents talk to models through the AIProvider interface. The default provider is heuristic: it requires no key and no network and fills findings from templates keyed on CWE. This keeps a base scan fully offline and deterministic, important for tests and air-gapped environments. Cloud (anthropic, openai) and local (ollama) providers are drop-in alternatives. If a requested provider is unavailable, the factory falls back to heuristic with a warning rather than failing the scan.

docs.title: Error handling philosophy
docs.text: A single broken component must not stop a scan. A scanner that raises is recorded in ScanResult.errors and the scan continues. An agent that fails on a finding falls back to heuristic enrichment for that finding. The goal is that nephilex scan always produces a usable report.

docs.title: Attack Simulation Mode
docs.text:
Most scanners stop at "this endpoint is vulnerable to SQL injection." Nephilex goes further: for each meaningful finding it produces a safe, self-contained demonstration of the weakness, aimed at the developer who owns the code.

Enable it with --attack-sim or attack_simulation: true in config.

docs.title: What it produces
docs.text:
For every finding at Medium severity or above, Nephilex generates an ExploitScenario with six parts:

  1. Discovery, how an attacker would find the weakness in the first place.
  2. Walkthrough, a step-by-step, read-only explanation of the exploit.
  3. Data at risk, what could actually be exposed or changed.
  4. Business impact, the consequence in plain language.
  5. How the fix blocks it, why the recommended remediation stops the attack.
  6. Before / after, a concise comparison of the vulnerable and fixed states.

These appear in the Markdown and HTML reports (in a collapsible section) and in the JSON output under each finding's exploit field.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
The simulation is descriptive, not executed:

  • Nephilex never sends traffic to a live target.
  • It never runs generated exploit code.
  • With a real model, the prompt constrains output to an educational, non-weaponized walkthrough rather than a copy-paste exploit.

Each scenario is marked sandbox_ok: true to record that it was produced in this isolated, non-executing context, and each simulation notes that no live target was contacted.

docs.title: With and without a model
docs.text:
• Offline (heuristic provider, the default): scenarios come from templates keyed on the finding's CWE. They are accurate for the common classes (SQLi, command injection, hardcoded secrets, and so on) and completely deterministic.
  • With a model (anthropic/openai/ollama): the agent writes a scenario tailored to the specific code, framework, and data flow, which reads more like a real penetration-test note. If the model call fails, Nephilex falls back to the template so the report is never left incomplete.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
For a SQL injection finding, the offline simulation reads roughly:

Discovery: Fuzz the parameter with a single quote. A resulting SQL error or changed response reveals the input reaches the query.

Walkthrough: 1. Observe a normal request. 2. Send ' OR '1'='1 in the parameter. 3. The WHERE clause becomes always-true, returning rows the user should not see. 4. Escalate with UNION SELECT to read other tables.

Data at risk: Any data reachable by the database user, often user records, password hashes, tokens, and PII.

How the fix blocks it: Parameterized queries bind input as data, so ' OR '1'='1 is treated as a literal string and the query structure can no longer change.

Run it yourself against the bundled example:

nephilex scan examples/vulnerable-app --attack-sim -f markdown -o report.md

docs.title: Audit log
docs.text:
Every fix Nephilex applies and every suppression that hides or accepts a finding is recorded in .nephilex/audit.log, inside the repository. The file is meant to be committed: it gives reviewers and auditors one place to answer "who suppressed this, when, and why" and "what did the automated fixes change".

Records are hash-chained, so nephilex audit verify detects a record that was edited, deleted, inserted or moved. Read What it proves before relying on it as evidence.

docs.title: What is recorded
docs.text:
Action When fix.applied nephilex fix (or apply_fixes) wrote a deterministic fix to a file. One record per fix. With --verify-with-tests, details.tests records the test result (passed; fixes whose tests did not pass are never applied). fix.pr_opened nephilex fix --open-pr opened a pull request for the fixes. One record per fix, with the PR URL. suppression.added Nephilex saw a suppression definition for the first time: an allowlist entry, a .nephilex/exceptions.yml entry, an inline nephilex-ignore comment (when it first hides a finding), or a baseline file. suppression.matched A suppression hid or accepted a finding. kind is allowlist, exception, inline or baseline.

Suppression events are recorded once per content: a suppression.matched record is keyed by kind, finding fingerprint and reason, and a suppression.added record by kind, selector and reason. Scanning the same code again adds nothing; changing the reason of a suppression records it again, because that is a new decision.

Suppression events are written only when the project configuration is trusted and the target is a local directory, the same rule that decides whether inline comments and exceptions are honoured at all (see Which configuration is trusted). Scans of cloned remotes, --config-from-ref runs, nephilex agent and nephilex mcp never write to the scanned tree.

Baseline filtering (--baseline on nephilex scan, nephilex import and nephilex review) runs in the command after the scan and is recorded under the same rule: one suppression.added per baseline file content and one suppression.matched per finding it hid. Other callers can use the nephilex.audit.record_baseline helper.

docs.title: Turning it off
docs.text: Set audit_log: false in .nephilex.yml, or NEPHILEX_AUDIT_LOG=off in the environment (also 0, false, no). Both also cover the fix.applied and fix.pr_opened records of nephilex fix.

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
JSON Lines, ASCII only, one record per line. Every record has the same keys, with null where a field does not apply:

{"action":"suppression.matched","actor":"Jane Developer <jane@example.com>",
 "details":{"line":12,"selector":"python-shell-true","severity":"high","until":null},
 "fingerprint":"patterns.python-shell-true|tools/run.py|5d41402abc4b",
 "hash":"9c1e...","kind":"inline","path":"tools/run.py",
 "prev_hash":"77ab...","reason":"command is a constant list","rule":"patterns.python-shell-true",
 "seq":42,"ts":"2026-10-22T09:14:03.120Z","v":1}

(Shown wrapped; in the file each record is one line.)

Field Meaning v Record format version, currently 1. seq Position in the chain, starting at 1. ts UTC time, millisecond precision. actor user.name <user.email> from git config, else GIT_AUTHOR_NAME/GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL, else the OS user name. action One of the actions above. kind For suppressions: allowlist, exception, inline, baseline. fingerprint The finding's stable fingerprint, the same value baselines and exceptions use. rule, path Rule id and project-relative path. reason The suppression's reason, or for fixes whether the fix was verified. details Extra context: line, selector, expiry, exception status and owner, branch, commit, PR URL. prev_hash hash of the previous record; 64 zeros for the first. hash SHA-256 of the record's canonical form.

docs.title: The hash chain
docs.text:
The canonical form of a record is its JSON with every key except hash, keys sorted, no whitespace (separators=(",", ":")), ASCII only. hash is the hex SHA-256 of those bytes. To check a record by hand in Python:

import hashlib, json

rec = json.loads(line)
body = {k: v for k, v in rec.items() if k != "hash"}
canon = json.dumps(body, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"), ensure_ascii=True)
assert hashlib.sha256(canon.encode("ascii")).hexdigest() == rec["hash"]

Each record's prev_hash must equal the previous record's hash, and seq must count up by one. Editing any field changes the hash; deleting, inserting or reordering a record breaks a prev_hash link or the seq count at that point.

docs.title: What is never written
docs.text: The log is committed, so it must not leak what the scanner found. Nephilex never writes code lines or finding snippets to it (fixes record rule, path, line, fingerprint and verification state only). Every string field is passed through the same secret masking the secrets scanner uses for report snippets, and credentials in URLs are removed, so a token pasted into a suppression reason is masked. Fields are capped at 500 characters.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
nephilex audit verify [PATH] [--anchor HASH] [--json]
nephilex audit show   [PATH] [--action A] [--kind K] [--rule R] [--path GLOB]
                          [--actor TEXT] [--fingerprint FP] [--since DATE]
                          [--until DATE] [-n N] [--json]
nephilex audit export [PATH] -f csv|json [-o FILE] [--action A] [--kind K]
                          [--since DATE] [--until DATE]

PATH is the project directory (default .) or the log file itself.

  • verify exits 0 and prints the record count and head hash when the chain is intact, and exits 1 naming the first broken record (line number, seq and what is wrong) otherwise. Without a log it exits 0, unless --anchor is given.
  • show lists records oldest first, filtered; -n 20 shows the last 20 matches; --json prints JSON Lines.
  • export -f json writes the matching records together with the chain's verification result; -f csv writes one row per record, with details as JSON and cells that a spreadsheet would evaluate as a formula prefixed with '.

docs.title: Concurrency and failure
docs.text:
Writers take an exclusive lock on the log (flock on Linux and macOS; on Windows a byte-range lock placed past the end of the file, so readers are never blocked), read the current head under the lock, and append all of their records in one write. Parallel scans and fixes therefore extend one chain instead of forking it. A writer waits up to 15 seconds for the lock.

The audit log never fails a scan or a fix. If the log cannot be written (the directory is read-only, .nephilex is not a directory, the lock times out, or the log or .nephilex is a symlink, which is refused so a hostile repository cannot redirect the append), the run continues and the problem is reported as a warning and in the report's project_summary.audit.warning. If the last line is damaged (for example a crash mid-write), new records are still appended on a fresh line and verify points at the damaged line.

docs.title: With nephilex fix
docs.text:
nephilex fix refuses to run on a working tree with uncommitted changes, with one exception: .nephilex/audit.log itself, because the scan that produced the findings may just have appended to it. The fix commit includes the log, so the fix.applied records travel with the fixes they describe. If .nephilex/ is ignored by git, the log is left out of the commit and a note says so (add !.nephilex/audit.log to .gitignore to commit it). If the fix fails and is rolled back, the log is restored to its state before the run.

fix.pr_opened is appended after the branch is pushed, so it is in the working tree of the fix branch, not in the pull request. Commit it with your next change.

docs.title: What it proves and what it does not
docs.text:
The log is tamper-evident, not tamper-proof.

It does show:

  • that no record in the middle of the chain was edited, removed, inserted or reordered since it was written, provided the chain verifies;
  • the order in which fixes and suppressions were recorded, and the reason given for each suppression at the time.

It does not show, on its own:

  • that nothing was removed from the end. Truncating the last records leaves a valid, shorter chain;
  • that the log was not rewritten. Anyone who can write the file can recompute every hash and produce a valid chain with different content;
  • who acted. actor comes from git config, which anyone can set; it is a claim, not an authenticated identity;
  • when. Timestamps come from the writer's clock;
  • that every suppression was recorded. Runs with the log disabled, untrusted runs, and suppressions applied by other tools are not in it.

To close the first two gaps, anchor the chain outside the repository: after each merge to the main branch, have CI run nephilex audit verify --json and store the head value somewhere the repository's writers cannot change (a CI artifact, a release note, a signed tag, a transparency log). Later, nephilex audit verify --anchor <stored head> fails unless that record is still in the chain, which catches truncation and wholesale rewrites. Git history helps too: the log is committed, so git log -p .nephilex/audit.log shows every change to it, and protected branches with signed commits make rewriting it visible. For identity, rely on your forge's authenticated commit and review records, and treat actor as a convenience.

docs.title: Benchmarks & accuracy
docs.text: A scanner's most important number is how accurate it is, and the most honest thing a young scanner can do is publish that number with its methodology, and republish it when it gets worse. Nephilex measures accuracy three ways: a small in-repo labeled corpus, public labeled datasets scored side by side with Bandit and Semgrep, and finding inventories on large reference apps.

docs.title: Labeled corpus (precision and recall)
docs.text:
A small, fully labeled corpus ships in the repo so the numbers are reproducible on any machine with one command and no downloads:

python benchmarks/accuracy.py

Every case is a single file that is either vulnerable (Nephilex must raise at least one actionable finding) or safe (Nephilex must raise none). From that:

  • Recall = caught vulnerable cases / all vulnerable cases (did we miss a bug?)
  • Precision = caught / (caught + findings on safe cases) (did we cry wolf?)

Current results:

Domain Recall Precision Vulnerable cases Safe cases False positives secrets 100% 100% 1 1 0 sast 100% 100% 7 9 0 taint 100% 100% 22 22 0 iac 100% 100% 1 1 0 llm 100% 100% 17 17 0 mcp 100% 100% 7 7 0 malware 100% 100% 4 5 0 overall 100% 100% 59 62 0

Read this number honestly

This is a small sanity-and-regression corpus (59 vulnerable, 62 safe cases), not a claim of 100% real-world accuracy. 100% here means Nephilex classifies every case in this set correctly, and the run exits non-zero if it does not, so a regression fails CI. On independent public datasets the numbers are far lower; see the next section.

The llm rows are worth calling out: there is no standard public benchmark for LLM/AI-application vulnerability classes (prompt injection, insecure model-output handling, unsafe model loading, secrets in prompts, excessive agency). This labeled set covers OWASP LLM01/02/05/06/08 with a vulnerable and a safe case each, so the accuracy claim in Nephilex's strongest and least-crowded domain is measurable and reproducible rather than asserted.

This corpus already earned its keep: building it surfaced two real bugs, both now fixed and covered by regression tests:

  • A false negative: subprocess(..., shell=True) was being dropped by the engine whenever the AST taint tier ran, because that tier does not model a taint-independent smell. Command-execution findings now survive.
  • A false positive: a properly parameterized query execute("... %s", (uid,)) was flagged as SQL injection because a tainted value in the bound-parameters argument counted. Bound parameters are now recognized as the safe form.

docs.title: Public labeled datasets (Nephilex, Bandit, Semgrep)
docs.text: The in-repo corpus is written by the same people who write the rules, so it cannot tell you how Nephilex does on code it was not tuned for. For that, Nephilex is scored on two independent, public, labeled Python datasets, next to Bandit and Semgrep run on the same files and scored by the same code.

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[ast]"                    # Nephilex with the AST tier
pip install bandit semgrep                 # ideally in a separate virtualenv
python benchmarks/public/run.py            # both datasets, all three tools

Useful variations:

python benchmarks/public/run.py --dataset owasp-python --tools nephilex,bandit,semgrep
python benchmarks/public/run.py --offline  # re-score cached outputs, no network, no tool runs
python benchmarks/public/run.py --bandit /path/to/bandit --semgrep /path/to/semgrep

--bandit and --semgrep (or the NEPHILEX_BENCH_BANDIT and NEPHILEX_BENCH_SEMGREP environment variables) point at tools installed outside the current environment. A tool that cannot be found is recorded as not_run with the reason; no numbers are produced for it.

Outputs:

  • benchmarks/results/public/<dataset>.json: dataset commit and archive hash, tool versions, run dates, command lines, the CWE mapping tables used, per-rule CWE inventory, and per-category and overall metrics for every tool and mode, including the list of false-positive and false-negative case ids.
  • benchmarks/results/public/SUMMARY.md: generated tables.
  • benchmarks/results/public/findings/<dataset>/<tool>.json: every finding normalized to file, line, rule id and CWEs (no source code), so the scoring can be audited or re-run with --offline without installing the tools.
  • benchmarks/.corpora/ (git-ignored): the downloaded datasets, the cached Semgrep ruleset and each tool's raw JSON output.

docs.title: Scoring
docs.text:
OWASP BenchmarkPython follows the OWASP Benchmark methodology. A test case is flagged when the tool reports at least one finding in that test case's source file (testcode/BenchmarkTestNNNNN.py) whose CWE matches the case's CWE. Findings in that file with a different CWE are ignored for that case; findings in helpers and templates are ignored. Flagged vulnerable case = TP, flagged safe case = FP, unflagged safe = TN, unflagged vulnerable = FN. Per category and overall: TPR (recall), FPR, precision, F1 and the OWASP score, TPR - FPR. Overall numbers are given two ways: pooled (counts summed over all 1230 cases, which weights large categories such as weakrand with 326 cases) and category average (unweighted mean of the per-category TPR, FPR and score, as on the official OWASP scorecard).

SecurityEval has no safe samples, so only recall can be measured. Precision, FPR and F1 are undefined and are not reported. A sample is detected when the tool reports a finding in its file with a matching CWE; the any mode also reports how many samples got any finding at all, whatever its CWE.

CWE matching comes in two modes, both always published:

  • strict: one of the tool's own reported CWEs equals the labeled CWE.
  • mapped: the tool's CWEs, plus documented per-rule overrides, intersect an equivalence group containing the label. The groups join parent and child CWEs (for example 327/328/916 for weak hashing, 22/23/36/73/99 for path traversal, 94/95 for code injection, 330/331/338 for weak randomness). They are in benchmarks/public/mapping.py and apply to every tool equally.

Manual overrides exist only where a tool reports a generic or wrong CWE for a rule with a single documented purpose. After auditing the per-rule inventory, the overrides are: Bandit's XML blacklist rules B313 to B320 and B405 to B410 (reported as CWE-20, mapped to CWE-611), B506 yaml_load (CWE-20 to CWE-502), B102 exec_used and B307 eval (reported as CWE-78, mapped to CWE-95), and Semgrep's python.flask.security.injection.tainted-sql-string (registry metadata says CWE-704, mapped to CWE-89). No Nephilex rule needed an override. Overrides only add CWEs. Note that they cut both ways: Bandit's mapped OWASP score is lower than its strict one, because the overrides credit rules that also fire on safe cases.

docs.title: Methodology checks
docs.text:
Corpus-specific keying. No rule refers to a benchmark file name, test id, helper module or function (helpers.*, the benchmark's request wrapper or HTML-escape helper), variable name, comment, or the expected-results CSV. An audit before publishing removed three things that were closer to the benchmark's own "safe" idioms than to general mitigations: the blocklist guards '../' in p (path traversal) and "contains no quote" (XPath), the .replace("'", ...) XPath sanitizer and the "quoted literal only" check before eval. Those blocklists are incomplete in general (an absolute path or another quoting style gets past them), so the engine no longer trusts them. That costs 66 OWASP false positives (16 path traversal, 38 XPath, 12 code injection), which are in the table above. os.path.exists and other existence checks were also dropped as path sinks after the false-positive check below, which costs 5 path-traversal true positives. One rule that is correct but was motivated by the benchmark stays and is documented: request.path is not a source in a Flask view whose routes have no <converters>, because routing has already fixed the path.

Split halves (not a held-out test). The OWASP score is stable across halves, but both halves were visible during development, so this shows the rules are not keyed to individual cases, not that they generalise:

Split Cases Mapped score (pooled) Mapped score (category avg) Strict score (pooled) even test numbers 615 +89.4 +92.2 +71.5 odd test numbers 615 +89.4 +89.0 +70.1 random half A (seed 20261022) 611 +88.8 +92.7 +70.9 random half B 619 +90.0 +90.2 +70.7

SecurityEval (a different corpus). Mapped recall went from 12/121 (9.9%) in 0.9.2 to 32/121 (26.5%). Five of the 32 come from rules added after reading SecurityEval's misses (compile() as a code sink, a redirect through headers["Location"], and lxml resolve_entities=True, three samples); the SQL-from-a-parameter rule was written for a SecurityEval sample named in the task (CWE-089_author_1.py). Without the five post-hoc detections the figure is 27/121 (22.3%). That is the better estimate of how the OWASP-driven work transfers to code it was not developed on: a large gain over 0.9.2, still behind Bandit on CWE-average recall (23.3%) and CWE breadth (21 CWEs).

False positives on code with no known vulnerabilities. The SAST, taint and auth scanners (ast-python, ast-python-xfile, patterns, authz) were run on Flask 3.0.3's tutorial and JavaScript example apps, the Flask 3.0.3 and Werkzeug 3.0.3 sources, and the installed click, requests, jinja2, rich and typer packages. Findings at severity low or above, 0.9.2 scanners against these changes:

Earlier drafts of this change were noisier on these projects (eval/exec of a function parameter in template engines, os.path.exists on environment paths, x.open() on test clients, http.cookiejar set_cookie(cookie) and set_cookie(..., **kwargs)); those rules were removed or narrowed before publishing.

docs.title: What changed since 0.9.2
docs.text:
Each fix below is a general rule meant to hold on real code. Details per rule are in Scanners.

  • Flow-sensitive taint. Branches, match, loops and try are analyzed separately and joined, so if not p: p = "" keeps the taint (the idiom behind 41 of the 80 false negatives in 0.9.2). Conditions that fold to a constant prune the dead branch. Literal dicts, lists and configparser objects are tracked per key.
  • Guards. Early returns on complete mitigations refine the value after them: allowlist membership, isdigit()-style checks, a urlparse(u).netloc allowlist, and a resolved-path containment check.
  • Sources. Methods that return request data (request wrappers) are sources when called on an object built from the request, in the same file or across files. request.path is not a source in a view whose routes have no converters.
  • New Python rules. Reflected XSS from view return values and Markup, |safe in templates, open redirect, XXE with external entities enabled, LDAP and XPath injection, trust boundary (session stores), weak randomness for tokens and session values, hashlib.new("md5"), pathlib file access, compile() as a code sink, and set_cookie() without secure=True (CWE-614) or httponly=True (CWE-1004).
  • Fewer sink-only findings. shell=True, os.system and pickle.loads whose payload is built only from literals are no longer reported. yaml.load with an unsafe loader is still reported, graded by taint.
  • Function parameters. SQL built by formatting a function parameter is reported at low confidence. The regex tier used to catch some of these, but the engine dropped its CWE-89 findings wherever the taint tier ran.

docs.title: What the numbers say
docs.text:
• On OWASP BenchmarkPython Nephilex now scores +89.4 pooled and +91.3 by category average (mapped), against +18.6 and +7.5 for Bandit and +14.2 and +6.0 for Semgrep. Because the rules were developed with this dataset visible and it is generated from a small set of templates, read this as "Nephilex handles the idioms in this benchmark", not as a real-world detection rate.
  • The 74 false positives are 66 cases guarded only by blocklist checks that Nephilex deliberately does not trust (see above), 5 yaml.load(..., Loader=yaml.Loader) calls on a constant document (an unsafe loader is still reported, at low severity, because it is wrong code even when today's input is constant), and 3 payloads that come from a wrapper method in another file returning a constant, which the regex tier, grading one file at a time, cannot see.
  • Strict mode (+70.8) is lower mainly because Nephilex reports MD5/SHA-1 as CWE-327 against the benchmark's CWE-328 label (71 cases) and eval/exec as CWE-95 against its parent CWE-94 (20 cases); the other 5 misses are the path-traversal cases whose only sink is an existence check.
  • On SecurityEval Nephilex ties Bandit on mapped recall (32 samples each) but trails it on CWE-average recall (18.4% vs 23.3%) and CWE breadth (17 vs 21 CWEs). Without the detections from rules added after reading SecurityEval, Nephilex is at 27 samples. SecurityEval covers many classes Nephilex has no Python rule for (hard-coded passwords as CWE-259, log injection, temporary files, regex DoS, SSRF), and most samples are helper functions with no web request.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Labeled-dataset bias. OWASP BenchmarkPython is synthetic: every case is generated from templates, uses Flask, and contains deliberate traps (dead branches, constant conditions, overwritten values) that reward or punish specific analysis features. Category sizes are uneven (326 weakrand cases, 16 sqli cases), which dominates the pooled numbers; the category average is published for that reason. Real applications look different.
  • SecurityEval has no negatives, so it cannot measure false positives at all, and most CWEs have one to six samples. Many samples are snippets whose input is a function parameter rather than a web request, which penalizes tools that require a proven untrusted source (the Nephilex taint tier) relative to tools that flag sinks unconditionally (Bandit).
  • CWE mapping caveats. Tools pick different CWEs for the same issue (MD5 is CWE-327 in Bandit, Semgrep and Nephilex, but the benchmark label is CWE-328), so strict understates every tool and mapped depends on the committed groups and overrides. Both are published; the mapping tables are embedded in each results file.
  • Python only. These datasets measure the Python SAST and taint tiers. They say nothing about Nephilex's JavaScript/TypeScript tiers, secrets, dependency, IaC, container or LLM-application scanners.
  • Default configurations only. Semgrep was run with the p/python registry ruleset on the Community Edition engine (no cross-file Pro analysis); another ruleset (for example p/default) or Semgrep Pro would give different numbers. Nephilex was run without an AI provider (--no-ai), so AI triage is not measured. Bandit and Semgrep were not tuned for these datasets. Nephilex's rules were revised after studying its OWASP misses, with no case held out (see "Methodology checks"); no rule refers to a benchmark file, test id, helper or generated name.
  • Single run, single machine. All three tools are deterministic for a fixed input, but the runs were made once, on Windows. Nephilex's default scanner set includes a dependency scanner that may query OSV for the dataset's requirements.txt; those findings fall outside the test cases and do not affect the scores.

docs.title: Held-out benchmark: real fix commits
docs.text: The public datasets above have a known weakness: Nephilex's Python rules were revised with OWASP BenchmarkPython visible. This benchmark answers that with code nobody tuned anything on: real vulnerabilities from real projects, taken as before/after pairs from the commits that fixed them. This is the frozen v1 set; a development set and a time-split test set use the same rule (see "Three benchmark sets" below).

docs.title: Selection rule
docs.text:
The rule was written down and committed (in benchmarks/heldout/selection.py, with the resulting manifest) before any tool was run on the selected files. Git history shows the order. In full:

  1. Source. GitHub Advisory Database, reviewed advisories only, ecosystems pip and npm, published from 2024-01-01 to 2026-09-30, not withdrawn.
  2. CWE. The advisory lists at least one CWE that Nephilex's Python or JavaScript/TypeScript source-code rules report, or a member of the equivalence group that contains one (benchmarks/public/mapping.py). The claimed CWEs, with the scanner modules that report them, are recorded in the manifest: 22, 73, 74, 77, 78, 79, 80, 89, 90, 94, 95, 295, 306, 327, 330, 338, 347, 352, 489, 501, 502, 598, 601, 611, 614, 639, 643, 918, 1004, 1336. With their groups the target set adds 23, 36, 88, 99, 297, 328, 331, 564, 776 and
  3. CWEs reported only by configuration, infrastructure, dependency, CI, secret, other-language or LLM-misuse rules (for example 200, 250, 732) are not claimed here: those rules detect them only in narrow contexts. A case's label is the subset of its advisory's CWEs that is in the target set.
  4. Fix commit. At least one advisory reference is a GitHub commit URL (/commit/<sha> or /pull/<n>/commits/<sha>). All such commits are used.
  5. Files. From each fix commit, every modified or renamed .py, .js, .mjs, .cjs, .jsx, .ts, .mts, .cts or .tsx file, except tests (test/tests/spec/__tests__/e2e directories, test_*.py, *_test.py, test.py, tests.py, conftest.py, *.test.js, *.spec.ts and similar), documentation and examples (doc, docs, example(s), sample(s)), vendored or build output (vendor, third_party, node_modules, dist, build, coverage, ...), minified or generated files (*.min.js, bundles, *_pb2.py) and TypeScript declarations (*.d.ts). Files the fix added or deleted have no before/after pair and are skipped. Within one advisory a path is taken once, from the first commit that touches it; a file and commit already used by another advisory is not used twice.
  6. Localized fixes. An advisory whose fix touches more than 5 eligible files is dropped as a refactor: most of its changed lines would not be the vulnerable code.
  7. Sampling. Candidate advisories are ordered by SHA-256 of their GHSA id, a fixed order nobody chose, and taken until 120 pip and 80 npm cases are reached. Nothing in the order depends on any tool.

A case is one file of one advisory. The vulnerable version is the file at the fix commit's first parent; the patched version is the file at the fix commit. The manifest (benchmarks/heldout/manifest.json) records for each case the advisory id, CVE, CWEs, repository, parent and fix SHAs, paths, the changed line ranges on both sides and the SHA-256 of both versions, so anyone can re-fetch and verify exactly the same files. It also lists every dropped advisory and file with its reason.

Changed lines come from the fix commit's unified diff: removed lines on the vulnerable side and added lines on the patched side. A hunk that only inserts lines marks the two vulnerable-side lines around the insertion point, and a hunk that only deletes marks the two patched-side lines around the deletion.

docs.title: Scoring
docs.text:
Fixed with the selection rule, before any tool ran:

  • Window. A finding belongs to a case when it is in the case's file and its line is within 3 lines of a changed line on that side. Windows of 0 and 10 lines are published as a sensitivity check.
  • CWE match. mapped (primary): the finding's CWEs, plus the documented rule overrides, intersect the equivalence group of one of the case's label CWEs, exactly as in the public benchmark (benchmarks/public/mapping.py, unchanged). strict: a finding CWE equals a label CWE. any: any finding in the window, whatever its CWE.
  • Detected. The vulnerable version has a matching finding in the window around its changed lines.
  • Flagged after the fix. The patched version has a matching finding in the window around its changed lines. Still flagged counts detected cases that are also flagged after the fix.
  • Recall = detected / cases. Fix-aware recall = (detected and not flagged after the fix) / cases: the tool told the vulnerable version apart from the patched one.
  • Precision proxy = detected / (detected + flagged after the fix), treating every match on fixed code as a false positive. Real advisories have no labeled safe code, so this is a proxy, not precision (see Limitations).
  • Results are given per case (file) and per advisory (an advisory is detected when any of its files is), by CWE, language and ecosystem, with raw counts. A case with two label CWEs counts once in each CWE row.

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[ast]"
pip install bandit semgrep                  # ideally in a separate virtualenv
python benchmarks/heldout/run.py fetch      # files in the manifest, verified by SHA-256
python benchmarks/heldout/run.py scan --bandit /path/to/bandit --semgrep /path/to/semgrep
python benchmarks/heldout/run.py score      # re-score the committed results, no tools, no network

select re-applies the rule to the live Advisory Database (--api-command or GITHUB_TOKEN for authenticated GETs); because GitHub adds, edits and withdraws advisories, reproducing the published numbers starts at fetch, from the committed manifest. Downloaded files go to benchmarks/.corpora/heldout/ (git-ignored); they are scanned as data and never imported or run.

Outputs, in benchmarks/results/heldout/:

  • heldout.json: Nephilex source commit, manifest hash, tool versions and command lines, Semgrep ruleset digests, the CWE mapping tables, and every metric for every tool and mode, with the window sensitivity.
  • cases/<case_id>.json: one file per case with its manifest entry, every finding each tool reported on both versions (line, rule id, CWEs; no source code) and each tool's outcome. score re-scores from these.
  • runs.json (run metadata) and SUMMARY.md (generated tables, including the per-CWE breakdown in any mode and per ecosystem).

docs.title: What the numbers say
docs.text:
• On real fix commits, all three tools find very little. Nephilex detects 4 of 201 cases (2.0%), the same count as Semgrep; Bandit detects 12 of its 118 Python cases (10.2%). Against the +89.4 OWASP score above, this is the number to quote for code Nephilex was not developed on.
  • Bandit's lead comes from flagging sinks without asking where the data came from. Six of its 12 detections are eval() (B307, credited to CWE-94/95 by the committed override), two are shell=True and two are SQL built by string formatting. Real library advisories often have a public function parameter as the attacker-controlled input, which a sink-only rule catches and a source-to-sink taint rule does not.
  • Where Nephilex detected, three of its four detections came from the regex patterns tier (child_process.exec in two JavaScript files, pickle.loads in LangChain's FAISS loader); the fourth is the low-confidence AST rule for SQL formatted from a non-constant value with no traced source (LlamaIndex DuckDB retriever). None of the four is a traced flow from an untrusted source to a sink, the analysis behind the OWASP results.
  • Misses worth reading include Parsl (%-formatted SQL from a Flask route parameter passed to pandas.read_sql_query) and PaddlePaddle (shell=True with an f-string of a URL parameter), both found by Bandit and Semgrep. They are recorded, not fixed: no Nephilex rule was changed because of this benchmark.
  • Flagged after the fix is rare for every tool in mapped mode. Nephilex's one case is the LangChain loader, where the fix kept pickle.loads behind an opt-in flag, so the finding is arguably still correct. In any mode, Nephilex matches 6 fixed files: besides that one, cookie-flag, OAuth state and race-hint findings near the changed lines of open-redirect and XSS fixes (they name other weaknesses), and a command-injection finding in the patched MLflow file of a code-injection advisory.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Single-file view. Each case is only the changed file, not the repository. A flow whose source is in another file (a route handler calling a helper) is invisible to every tool. This handicaps taint-based analysis (Nephilex, Semgrep's taint rules) more than sink-only rules (Bandit).
  • Changed lines are a proxy for the vulnerable lines. A fix can add a check far from the sink, or touch several files of which one holds the bug. The window, the 5-file cap and the per-advisory roll-up limit this, they do not remove it.
  • The precision proxy is not precision. A match on the patched lines may still be a real issue (as in the LangChain case), and findings outside the changed lines are not counted at all, so a tool that reports a lot elsewhere in the file pays nothing. There is no labeled safe code in this benchmark.
  • Advisory CWE labels are noisy. Authors pick broad (CWE-74) or neighbouring CWEs; the any mode is published for that reason.
  • Small sample. 201 cases from 117 advisories, with most CWEs under 15 cases and none for CWE-611. Per-CWE rows are anecdotes, not rates.
  • Snapshot. The Advisory Database changes; the manifest freezes the 2026-10-23 selection. The selection rule was amended once before any score existed (see "Amendment" above).
  • Default configurations only, as in the public benchmark: Semgrep CE with two registry rulesets, Bandit defaults, Nephilex without AI triage. Semgrep timed out on some rules for 22 large case versions.

docs.title: After the Python detection work
docs.text:
Development data, not a claim, and no longer unseen: the Python rules for path traversal, XSS, SSRF and code injection, and library mode (see Scanners), were written after reading every Python miss in this set. Nephilex was re-run on the same 351 cases with scan --set dev --only nephilex, which keeps the committed Bandit and Semgrep results; the Nephilex source is commit 26011609fa7e31854e0a55dae887054af3d6137d (src/nephilex unmodified; benchmarks/results/dev/ now holds the combined run below; the library-mode run records 261c48999c9ca36ee4c6992ddc0d792a816341ac, a documentation commit with the same src/nephilex). The library-mode run used --nephilex-config with library_mode: "on" and --variant library-on; its results are in benchmarks/results/dev-library-on/. In the default configuration library mode stays off on these cases (auto needs a package manifest, and each case is a single file).
