All languages, mapped: Nephilex 14 of 351 (4.0%), flagged after the fix 4, fix-aware 10, against 12 / 4 / 8 at 0.11.0; JavaScript and TypeScript are unchanged (2 of 158). By CWE over all languages, detected / cases: CWE-22 1/40 (was 0/40), CWE-79 0/60 (0/60), CWE-918 1/64 (0/64), CWE-94 1/31 (1/31), CWE-95 1/8 (1/8). With library mode on: 23 of 351 (6.6%), flagged after the fix 4, fix-aware 19; CWE-22 4/40, CWE-79 1/60, CWE-918 1/64, CWE-94 3/31, CWE-95 4/8.

What changed and why the gain is small:

  • New detections, default mode: an SSRF through a FastAPI Query() parameter into aiohttp.ClientSession().get() (rembg) and a path traversal from a FastAPI UploadFile.filename into open() (libre-chat). Both fixes are recognized (a URL validator that checks is_private and friends, werkzeug.utils.safe_join), so neither is flagged after the fix.
  • Library mode adds nine vulnerable versions, none flagged after the fix: eval of text a library builds from its caller's data (Amazon Redshift driver vector parsing, OpenStack Vitrage query predicates, two Agno files reading a type name from a caller's dict, a llama-index streaming generator that evaluates server events), path traversal where a library joins a caller's name under its own directory (AGiXT safe_join, Banks prompt registry), a tar archive extracted without a filter (MONAI), and Wagtail's mark_safe of an f-string in a template tag. Bandit's sink-only eval rule finds all five of the code-injection cases, which is where much of its lead on this set came from.
  • Most target cases are out of reach of a single-file taint engine. Of the 106 Python cases labelled 22, 79, 918, 94, 95 or 1336, most change a file that holds neither the source nor the sink: version bumps, settings, a validator in a helper module, allowlist or authorization logic, IP canonicalization or DNS-rebinding pinning on an existing check, or HTML built from data (a parsed APK manifest, an exception, a traceback) that is not modeled as untrusted. Others are logic fixes (Weblate and gradio path handling, litellm request field checks) that no source-to-sink rule describes. Rules keyed to those projects would not generalize, so none were written.
  • Findings outside the changed lines. In the default run, Python findings rose from 473 to 505 over both versions (path traversal 22 to 39 on vulnerable files, open redirect 13 to 14, one new SSRF; XSS fell from 19 to 15 after route returns of jsonify and TemplateResponse stopped counting as HTML). Reading them: a zip-slip extraction in Weblate's backup restore (member names checked only with normpath) and a reflected XSS in a changedetection.io Flask route (the very bug of that advisory, but outside its changed lines) are real; a flow through an imported safe_join_path helper (xiaomusic) is most likely a false positive, because a helper in another file is not summarized; gradio's file route has its own allowlist logic that is not modeled.
  • Flagged after the fix stays at the baseline's 4 cases: SQL built with an f-string in two LangGraph SQLite checkpoint files, an open redirect in a Khoj auth router, and pickle.loads in the pdfminer CMap loader. None is in the CWE classes this work targeted, and the rules that report them did not change. Library mode flags the same four.

False-positive check (the projects and scanners of "False positives on code with no known vulnerabilities" above, findings at severity low or above, same Flask 3.0.3 sources; click 8.5.0, requests 2.34.2, jinja2 3.1.6, rich 15.0.0 and typer 0.27.3 installed on 2026-10-23):

Project 0.11.0 Now (auto) Library mode on Flask tutorial app (flaskr) 0 0 0 (auto keeps it off: Flask() entry point) Flask JavaScript example 0 0 0 (auto keeps it off) Flask 3.0.3 3 2 7 Werkzeug 3.0.3 7 7 9 click 0 0 0 requests 0 0 0 jinja2 1 1 6 rich 1 1 1 typer 0 0 0

The installed packages have no manifest in their directories, so auto leaves library mode off on them; the last column forces it on. Flask loses flask shell's exec of the PYTHONSTARTUP file, whose content was counted as tainted only because its file name was (compile() now takes taint from its source alone). Werkzeug's reloader and rich's pty.spawn demo stay, now at low confidence as operator input. The weak-hash findings that remain all sit in security code (session signing, the debugger PIN) and keep their severity. Library mode adds 12 low-confidence public-api findings, none counted by --fail-on: Flask's open_resource, open_instance_resource, Config.from_pyfile and Config.from_file, which join a caller's name under the app's root by design; two HTML fragments in Werkzeug's debugger repr that embed repr() text; and in jinja2 the file-system bytecode cache (names built from a bucket key), PackageLoader.get_source (whose split_template_path check is not modeled) and the traceback rewriter's exec of a code object. Reviewers of a library should expect findings of this kind.

docs.title: With all 0.12 detection work combined
docs.text:
Development data, not a claim. Nephilex re-run on the same 351 cases at commit 1692d69164140f534ac2f87f76cc3010b386d3fa, which combines the Python work above with the JavaScript/TypeScript taint engine, the authorization and malware precision fixes and the instruction-file rules (Bandit and Semgrep results kept, default configuration). The results are in benchmarks/results/dev/.

Subset Cases 0.11.0 Combined All languages 351 12 / 4 24 / 5 Python 193 10 / 4 12 / 4 JavaScript and TypeScript 158 2 / 0 12 / 1

Detected / flagged after the fix, mapped CWE match, 3-line window. Every case's result equals that of the separate Python and JavaScript/TypeScript runs, so the two kinds of work do not interact. The scan took 859 s against 735 s for 0.11.0 on the same machine.

After the precision fixes that followed (JavaScript/TypeScript containment checks, example code at low confidence, same-site redirect targets), a rerun at d00bdf64e1a939a9724a36740c6bd990d1b39302 detects the same 24 of 351 with 5 flagged after the fix; the only per-case change is a MobSF redirect to f"/download/{file_name}", no longer reported as an open redirect because its literal start keeps it on the same site.

docs.title: Public reference apps (finding inventory)
docs.text:
The larger harness scans real, known-vulnerable applications:

python benchmarks/run_benchmarks.py            # all available corpora
python benchmarks/run_benchmarks.py juice-shop # just one

It publishes a finding inventory (counts by scanner and severity, plus scan time) for OWASP Juice Shop, DVWA, WebGoat, and (with a manual download) NIST SARD/Juliet. An inventory is not precision/recall, it needs a ground-truth mapping per corpus, which is tracked as a ground_truth hook and where contributions are welcome, but it shows coverage shape and catches per-release regressions in what Nephilex finds and how fast.

docs.title: Methodology and honesty notes
docs.text:
• Runs are deterministic and offline (--no-ai, caching disabled) so numbers are comparable across machines.
  • Numbers that get worse are published anyway. A benchmark that only ever improves is marketing, not measurement.
  • The labeled corpus is intentionally small and unambiguous. Growing it (more languages, more classes, adversarial safe cases) directly improves the quality signal, and pull requests that add labeled cases are among the most valuable contributions to the project.

docs.title: CI/CD integration
docs.text: Nephilex is built to run in a pipeline: it emits SARIF for code-scanning platforms and can fail a build on a severity threshold.

docs.title: The official Action (recommended)
docs.text:
The fastest path is the official Action, one block of YAML:

name: Security
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read
  security-events: write   # required for the SARIF upload

jobs:
  nephilex:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0     # full history enables diff-aware PR scanning
      - uses: nephilex/nephilex@v0.11.0
        with:
          fail-on: high      # block merges on newly introduced High+ findings

That is the whole setup. Findings appear as PR annotations and in the Security tab. On pull requests the Action is diff-aware by default: it scans the base branch to build a baseline and gates only on findings the PR introduces, the property that keeps a first adoption from drowning in pre-existing alerts.

All inputs are optional; the useful ones:

Input Default Purpose path . Directory to scan fail-on (never fail) Severity gate: critical/high/medium/low fail-on-error (fail when fail-on is set) true or false to always or never fail when a scanner crashes scanners / exclude-scanners all Choose scanners min-severity (none) Report floor config (none) Path to a .nephilex.yml pr-config-from-base true On pull requests, read Nephilex config from the base branch so a PR cannot relax its own gate diff-aware true Baseline PRs against the base branch pr-comment false Post findings the PR introduces as an inline review upload-sarif true Upload to Code Scanning nephilex-version (the action's own version) Install a specific nephilex version from PyPI instead extra-args (none) Anything else nephilex scan accepts

docs.title: Pin the Action by commit
docs.text:
A tag such as v0.11.0 is a pointer, and on GitHub a pointer can in principle be moved to other code. Nephilex's release tags are protected against that, but a security gate in your pipeline should not depend on someone else's repository settings. Pin the full commit SHA, and keep the tag as a comment so you can see the version:

      - uses: nephilex/nephilex@9a03d39553e8dc9c42c548d7dc2b0596e6535d6e # v0.11.0

That is the commit v0.11.0 points to; check it with git ls-remote https://github.com/nephilex/nephilex refs/tags/v0.11.0. Dependabot's github-actions updates understand this form and move both the SHA and the comment when a new release comes out. Do the same for the other actions in the workflow (actions/checkout and so on).

docs.title: Hand-rolled workflow
docs.text:
If you need more control, a ready-to-copy workflow lives at .github/workflows/nephilex-scan.yml. It runs Nephilex, writes SARIF, and uploads it to GitHub Code Scanning so findings appear as PR annotations and in the Security tab.

To block merges instead of only annotating, add a gate:

      - name: Run Nephilex (gate on High+)
        run: nephilex scan . --fail-on high --quiet -f sarif -o nephilex.sarif

--fail-on high makes the step exit non-zero when any High or Critical finding is present.

docs.title: Diff-aware scanning with a baseline
docs.text: Adopting a scanner on an existing codebase usually means drowning in pre-existing findings. Nephilex supports two diff-aware modes:

docs.title: Git-native diff (--diff)
docs.text:
Report only findings on lines/files changed in a git range, plus dependency findings on changed lockfiles:

nephilex scan . --diff origin/main...HEAD --fail-on high
nephilex dependencies . --diff origin/main...HEAD
nephilex sbom . --diff origin/main...HEAD -o sbom-diff.json
nephilex supply-chain . --diff origin/main...HEAD --fail-on high

This also enables the dependency-diff scanner (version changes + npm behavior anomalies) automatically.

docs.title: Baseline fingerprint diff (--baseline)
docs.text:
# 1. Scan the base branch and save the report as a baseline (outside the tree).
nephilex scan /path/to/base-checkout -f json -o /tmp/baseline.json --quiet

# 2. Scan the PR, suppressing anything already in the baseline, and gate on new High+.
nephilex scan . --baseline /tmp/baseline.json --fail-on high --quiet

Findings are matched by a content-based fingerprint (the whitespace-normalized offending code, not the line number), so a finding is still recognized as pre-existing after unrelated edits shift it up or down the file. The shipped nephilex-scan.yml workflow does this automatically on pull requests.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text: Nephilex walks files in a deterministic, sorted order, so finding IDs and report ordering are stable across machines and runs, safe to diff report-to-report.

docs.title: Untrusted targets
docs.text: When scanning a remote repository (a git URL), Nephilex ignores any .nephilex.yml inside that repo by default, so a scanned project cannot weaken its own scan. Pass --trust-remote-config to opt in when you control the repository.

docs.title: GitLab CI
docs.text:
nephilex:
  image: python:3.12-slim
  script:
    - pip install nephilex
    - nephilex scan . -f sarif -o gl-nephilex.sarif --fail-on high
  artifacts:
    when: always
    paths:
      - gl-nephilex.sarif

docs.title: Bitbucket Pipelines
docs.text:
# bitbucket-pipelines.yml
pipelines:
  default:
    - step:
        name: Nephilex security scan
        image: python:3.12-slim
        script:
          - pip install nephilex
          - nephilex scan . -f sarif -o nephilex.sarif --fail-on high --no-ai --quiet
        artifacts:
          - nephilex.sarif

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
An official image is published to GHCR on every release, useful where pip is unavailable in CI or you want a pinned, reproducible scanner:

docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" ghcr.io/nephilex/nephilex scan /work --fail-on high

The image runs as a non-root user and includes git, so remote repository targets (nephilex scan https://github.com/org/repo) work too.

docs.title: Pre-commit hook
docs.text:
Nephilex ships hooks for the pre-commit framework, so catching a secret before it enters git history takes three lines:

# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/nephilex/nephilex
    rev: v0.11.0
    hooks:
      - id: nephilex-secrets        # fast, secrets-only, made for every commit
      # - id: nephilex              # full static scan, heavier; consider pre-push

nephilex-secrets runs only the secrets scanner with AI enrichment disabled, so it stays fast enough for every commit. The full nephilex hook is better suited to stages: [pre-push] or CI.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 Scan completed; no finding met the --fail-on threshold (or none was set). 1 Scan completed but a finding met the --fail-on threshold. 2 The target could not be resolved (bad path/URL, clone failed).

docs.title: Keeping scans fast in CI
docs.text:
• Restrict scanners to what you need: -s secrets,dependencies,patterns.
  • Disable AI enrichment for speed with --no-ai (findings still carry their built-in reasoning and taxonomy).
  • Use exclude_paths in .nephilex.yml to skip vendored or generated code.

docs.title: Scan your own CI/CD pipelines
docs.text:
Use the focused command to gate risky workflow changes without a full scan:

- name: CI/CD security
  run: nephilex cicd . --fail-on high --quiet

For Docker, Compose, and Kubernetes manifests: nephilex container . --fail-on high.

For Terraform and CloudFormation: nephilex cloud . --fail-on high.

Details: infrastructure-scanning.md.

docs.title: How Nephilex compares
docs.text: Nephilex is not trying to beat every specialist at its own game. The tools below are excellent, and if one of them is your whole problem, use it. Nephilex's bet is different: one tool across the domains, that explains and fixes, and keeps your code on your machine. Here is the honest version.

docs.title: Where the specialists are stronger
docs.text:
Tool What it is genuinely better at Semgrep A huge, battle-tested SAST rule ecosystem and community rules; deep per-language coverage; a mature registry. If SAST rule breadth is the whole job, Semgrep leads. Trivy Container and image scanning, a mature and fast SCA, wide adoption, and a large maintainer team. For container-first workflows it is the default. Snyk A large curated vulnerability database, first-class IDE and PR integrations, developer UX, and enterprise features (SSO, reporting, policies). GitGuardian / TruffleHog Dedicated secrets coverage, real-time monitoring, and validated detectors at scale.

Nephilex does not out-feature these in their home turf, and it says so.

docs.title: Where Nephilex is different
docs.text: Property Nephilex Typical specialist Domains in one pass Secrets, SCA, SAST, taint, IaC, and LLM together, one severity model, one report Usually one or two domains; you stitch several tools together Explanation Every finding: why, attacker path, business impact, CWE/OWASP Often a rule id and a line number Fixes Deterministic, self-verified fixes that open a PR Varies; many stop at detection AI / LLM coverage First-class OWASP-LLM-Top-10 scanner Emerging or absent Privacy Offline by default; code never leaves the machine unless you opt into a cloud model Often cloud-first Model Open-source core (Apache-2.0), self-hostable Often proprietary / SaaS

docs.title: When to choose Nephilex
docs.text:
• You want one tool across code, dependencies, secrets, IaC, and AI, instead of five dashboards and five bills.
  • You want findings your developers will actually act on, because each one is explained and often comes with the fix.
  • You are building AI/LLM-heavy applications and want that class of risk covered in the same pass.
  • You need the scanner to run offline / self-hosted for privacy or compliance reasons.

docs.title: When to choose something else
docs.text:
• You need the deepest possible SAST rule coverage for one language today: reach for Semgrep.
  • Your problem is container images and registries at scale: reach for Trivy.
  • You need enterprise ASPM (SSO, policy engine, ticketing, dashboards) right now: a commercial platform will serve you better while Nephilex matures.

Honest positioning is the point. Nephilex is a strong, unified, explainable, self-hostable scanner and fixer, in early alpha, that is especially good for AI-era codebases. Pick the tool that fits the job.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Nephilex reads configuration from, in increasing precedence:

  1. Built-in defaults.
  2. .nephilex.yml (or .nephilex.yaml) in the project root.
  3. A file passed with --config.
  4. Command-line flags.

Generate a starter file with nephilex init.

docs.title: Full reference
docs.text:
# Scanners to run. Empty = every scanner that applies to the project.
scanners: []            # e.g. ["secrets", "patterns"]

# Scanners to skip (applied after the list above).
exclude_scanners: []    # e.g. ["iac"]

# Extra path globs to ignore, added to the built-in ignore list
# (.git, node_modules, venv, build artifacts, etc.).
exclude_paths: []       # e.g. ["tests/fixtures/*", "*.min.js"]

# In a git work tree, untracked files that .gitignore (or .git/info/exclude)
# ignores are skipped; tracked files are always scanned. true scans the
# ignored files too. CLI: --include-ignored. See "Files that are scanned".
include_ignored: false

# Minimum severity to report: info | low | medium | high | critical
min_severity: info

# Exit non-zero if any finding is at/above this severity. Empty = never fail.
# Use this to gate CI.
fail_on: ""             # e.g. high

# Fail the run when a scanner crashes. Unset (the default) means: fail whenever
# fail_on is set, because a crashed scanner reports nothing and a gate must not
# read that as a pass. CLI: --fail-on-error / --no-fail-on-error.
# fail_on_error: true

# Attack Simulation Mode: safe, sandboxed exploit demonstrations per finding.
attack_simulation: false

# Generate fix patches (and verify the deterministic ones). Nephilex's
# deterministic, verified fixes are attached even with AI enrichment off
# (--no-ai); only model-proposed drafts need a provider.
generate_patches: false

# Reuse cached findings for unchanged files (content-hash keyed; file-local
# scanners only). CLI: --no-cache. See docs/performance.md.
cache: true

# Run scanners concurrently. Reports are deterministic either way.
parallel: true

# Record fixes and suppressions (allowlist entries, exceptions, inline
# nephilex-ignore comments, baselines) in the hash-chained .nephilex/audit.log.
# Trusted local projects only. NEPHILEX_AUDIT_LOG=off also turns it off.
# See docs/audit-log.md.
audit_log: true

# Python library mode: auto | on | off (default auto). In library mode the
# parameters of public functions are taint sources, and their findings are
# reported at low confidence, tagged public-api, and do not count toward
# fail_on. auto turns it on for a project with pyproject.toml, setup.py or
# setup.cfg and no recognized web application entry point. Quote "on" and
# "off" (bare on/off are YAML booleans, which are also accepted).
# See docs/scanners.md, "Library mode".
library_mode: auto

ai:
  # heuristic (offline, default) | anthropic | openai | ollama (local)
  provider: heuristic
  model: ""             # provider-specific; empty uses the provider default
  enabled: true         # false disables all AI enrichment
  temperature: 0.0
  max_tokens: 4096
  max_findings: 25      # only the highest-risk findings go to a model; the rest
                        # get offline reasoning (keeps CI runs bounded)

# Per-scanner options, keyed by scanner name.
scanner_options:
  secrets:
    entropy: true             # enable high-entropy string detection
    entropy_threshold: 4.0    # bits; raise to reduce false positives
    verify: false             # opt-in live check (CLI: --verify-secrets)
  dependencies:
    online: true              # query the OSV database for real, current CVEs
    timeout: 15               # seconds for OSV lookups
    cache: true               # cache OSV records on disk to speed repeat scans
    reachability: false       # experimental: imported/not-imported (Python + npm)
    symbol_reachability: false  # tier-2: Python symbol usage vs OSV hints
  supply-chain:
    online_intel: true        # fetch the feeds in NEPHILEX_INTEL_FEED, if any
  dependency-diff:
    ref: ""                   # git ref for PR diff (set by --diff / supply-chain)
    behavior: true            # npm registry metadata anomaly checks
    sandbox: auto             # auto | host | docker for metadata fetch
  provenance:
    require_for_releases: false

# Security policies - see docs/policy.md
policies: []

docs.title: Files that are scanned
docs.text:
Nephilex walks the target directory and skips the directories that are noise for security analysis (.git, node_modules, vendor, dist, build, virtual environments, caches) and anything matching exclude_paths.

When the target is inside a git work tree, Nephilex also asks git which untracked files it ignores (git ls-files --others --ignored --exclude-standard, run with the same hardening as every other git call) and skips them: build output, local virtual environments, editor and assistant folders such as .claude/, a local .env. What is scanned matches what git would commit:

  • Tracked files are always scanned, even when a .gitignore pattern matches them. Ignore rules only apply to untracked files, so a pull request cannot hide committed code by adding a pattern to .gitignore.
  • Untracked files that are not ignored (new files you have not added yet) are scanned.
  • Outside a git work tree, when git is not installed, or when the target directory is itself ignored, every file is walked as before.

--include-ignored (or include_ignored: true) scans the ignored files too, as earlier releases did. Files over 2 MB and symlinks that point outside the project are skipped either way.

docs.title: Secret verification (opt-in)
docs.text: --verify-secrets (or scanner_options.secrets.verify: true) makes a single, read-only call per detected secret to confirm whether it is actually live, GitHub, Stripe, Slack, OpenAI, and Google keys are supported; others report as unverified. A confirmed-live credential is escalated to Critical; a rejected one is downgraded. This makes authenticated network requests with the candidate credential, so it is off by default, restricted to local targets (never a cloned remote repo), and deliberately absent from the shipped CI templates. The secret value is used only for the request, it is never written to a finding, the cache, or a report.

docs.title: Runtime posture checks (--live-target)
docs.text: --live-target <url> runs a safe, read-only posture pass against a deployed URL alongside the static scan (or scan a URL directly with nephilex scan <url>): it checks security headers, cookie flags, HTTP-vs-HTTPS transport, version disclosure, and a short allowlist of exposed sensitive paths. It is non-intrusive, only GETs, no payloads or exploitation, but still: only point it at systems you are authorized to assess. It is a pre-DAST layer, not a crawler or fuzzer.

docs.title: Dependency scanning and OSV
docs.text:
The dependency scanner checks your declared packages against the public OSV database, which covers thousands of advisories across ecosystems. Only package names and versions are sent to OSV, never your source code, so this preserves Nephilex's offline-first stance. Set scanner_options.dependencies.online: false to use only the small bundled seed (fully offline); Nephilex also falls back to the seed automatically if OSV is unreachable.

Lookups are batched (no dependency is silently dropped), retried with backoff on transient failures, and cached on disk so repeat scans are fast. The cache lives under ~/.cache/nephilex/osv by default; override it with the NEPHILEX_CACHE_DIR environment variable, or disable it with scanner_options.dependencies.cache: false.

docs.title: Reachability (experimental)
docs.text:
Most dependency alerts concern packages your code never even imports. With --reachability (or scanner_options.dependencies.reachability: true), Nephilex annotates each PyPI dependency finding with an import-level verdict: imported (first-party code imports the package, treat as actionable) or not imported (no import found, deprioritized to an unlikely likelihood, but never suppressed, since dynamic imports and framework hooks are not traced). The verdict appears in the finding description and as reachability in finding metadata in JSON/SARIF reports. Supported for Python and npm at import level; add --symbol-reachability for Python symbol-level hints when OSV provides them.

See also policy.md for the policy engine.

docs.title: Code scanning: two tiers
docs.text:
Nephilex scans source code with two complementary scanners:

  • patterns (always on), a fast, regex-based pass with a lightweight single-hop taint check. Broad language coverage, catches the common cases.
  • ast-python and ast-js (optional), tree-sitter data-flow analyzers for Python and JavaScript/TypeScript that track tainted values through multiple variable hops, so they catch injection the regex tier misses (e.g. x = req.query.id, then y = x, then db.query('... ' + y)). They also avoid the regex tier's common false positives: a parameterized query (db.query('... WHERE id = ?', [id])) and sanitized values (DOMPurify.sanitize(...), Number(...), secure_filename(...)) are treated as safe. Enable with:
pip install "nephilex[ast]"

Without the extra, the AST scanners report as not-applicable and Nephilex uses the regex tier, nothing breaks. When both tiers run, findings for the same weakness are de-duplicated (the higher-confidence AST finding wins), so you never see one issue reported twice.

docs.title: Library mode (library_mode)
docs.text:
Value Effect auto (default) On when the scan root has pyproject.toml, setup.py or setup.cfg and no web application entry point is found (Flask(), FastAPI(), Starlette(), get_wsgi_application() and the others listed in Scanners); off otherwise on Always on, for example for a library whose repository also ships a demo app off Never on

Any other value is a configuration error (exit 2), like the other keys. YAML reads a bare on/off as true/false; both forms are accepted. The JSON report records the decision under project_summary.library_mode (setting, active, reason). Library-mode findings carry the tag public-api, are low confidence and never fail fail_on; the reasoning is in Scanners.

docs.title: Common recipes
docs.text:
Fast secrets-and-deps check, fail the build on High+:

scanners: [secrets, dependencies]
fail_on: high

Everything, with the flagship features, using a local model:

attack_simulation: true
generate_patches: true
ai:
  provider: ollama
  model: llama3.1

Quiet down a noisy entropy scanner:

scanner_options:
  secrets:
    entropy_threshold: 4.5

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Credentials for cloud providers and git hosts are read from the environment (see .env.example):

Variable Used by ANTHROPIC_API_KEY anthropic provider OPENAI_API_KEY openai provider OLLAMA_HOST ollama provider (default http://localhost:11434) GITHUB_TOKEN / GITLAB_TOKEN opening pull requests with nephilex fix --open-pr NEPHILEX_AI_MODEL model override for the configured provider NEPHILEX_AI_TIMEOUT / NEPHILEX_AI_MAX_RETRIES per-call model timeout in seconds (default 60) and retries (default 2) NEPHILEX_GIT_TIMEOUT timeout for git commands in seconds (default 300) NEPHILEX_CACHE_DIR cache location for scan results and OSV data NEPHILEX_INTEL_FEED comma-separated HTTPS URLs of your own malicious-package lists, merged with the bundled one (none by default) NEPHILEX_DAST_URL target for dynamic checks (same as --live-target) NEPHILEX_MCP_ROOTS / NEPHILEX_MCP_SCAN_TIMEOUT directories the MCP server may scan, and its scan timeout (default 600) NEPHILEX_DASHBOARD_TOKEN / NEPHILEX_DASHBOARD_ALLOWED_HOSTS / NEPHILEX_DASHBOARD_MAX_SCANS dashboard access control and retention, see Web dashboard NEPHILEX_WATCH_KEEP_SNAPSHOTS number of nephilex watch snapshots kept per target (default 50)

docs.title: Which configuration is trusted
docs.text:
The scanned repository is treated as untrusted input, because in CI it is often a pull request from someone outside your team. Its configuration could otherwise exclude every path, switch scanners off, or allowlist its own findings.

Situation .nephilex.yml, .nephilex/rules, .nephilex/exceptions.yml, .nephilex/context.yml, nephilex-ignore comments Local path (nephilex scan .) Honoured Cloned remote (nephilex scan https://...) Ignored unless --trust-remote-config --config-from-ref REF .nephilex.yml and .nephilex/context.yml read from that git ref; the checked-out tree is untrusted, so its rules, exceptions and comments are ignored --config PATH That file is always honoured (you chose it) nephilex agent, nephilex mcp The monitored or scanned directory is never trusted

.nephilex/context.yml declares sanitizers and trusted sources that switch checks off, so it follows the same rule as .nephilex.yml; see Project context. The audit log is written only when the project is trusted and local.

For pull requests, use --config-from-ref origin/<base-branch> so the gate uses the configuration already merged on the base branch. The GitHub Action does this automatically (pr-config-from-base, on by default).

docs.title: CLI flags
docs.text:
Every relevant config field has a flag, which overrides the file:

nephilex scan TARGET
  -c, --config PATH         path to a .nephilex.yml config file
  -s, --scanners a,b        run only these scanners
      --exclude a,b         skip these scanners
  -f, --format FMT          output format (repeatable): table json sarif markdown html csv
  -o, --output PATH         write reports (a directory writes one file per format)
      --baseline PATH       report only findings not present in a saved JSON report
      --ai-provider NAME    heuristic | anthropic | openai | ollama
      --ai-model ID         model override
      --no-ai               disable AI enrichment
      --include-ignored     also scan untracked files that git ignores
      --attack-sim          enable Attack Simulation Mode
      --patches             generate/verify fix patches (deterministic ones also with --no-ai)
      --min-severity SEV    report findings at/above this severity
      --fail-on SEV         non-zero exit if any finding is at/above this severity
      --[no-]fail-on-error  fail (or not) when a scanner crashes
      --live-target URL     run safe, read-only posture checks against a URL you own
  -b, --branch NAME         branch to clone for remote targets
      --trust-remote-config load .nephilex.yml from a cloned remote repo (off by default)
      --config-from-ref REF read config from a git ref; treat the tree as untrusted
  -q, --quiet               suppress progress output

docs.title: Project context
docs.text:
A scanner sees code, not your architecture. It cannot know that myapp.security.escape_html is your reviewed HTML encoder, that scripts/ only runs from an operator's laptop, or that billing/ holds card data. .nephilex/context.yml tells it, so findings reflect your project instead of a generic one:

  • sanitizers: functions that neutralise taint, per language and optionally per CWE. The AST taint tiers (ast-python, ast-js) stop reporting flows that pass through them.
  • trusted_sources: values that are not attacker-controlled, such as an internal configuration reader. Flows that start there are not reported.
  • internal_paths: code that is not reachable from outside. Findings there are lowered one severity level and tagged internal. They are never hidden.
  • exposure: per-path notes that raise or lower likelihood.
  • data_classification: paths or models that hold sensitive data. Findings there are raised one severity level.

Every finding the context changes says so in metadata["context"], and every flow it clears is listed in the scan summary, so a reviewer can see exactly what the file did. See Reviewing what the context changed.

docs.title: Trust rules
docs.text:
The context file is project configuration and follows the same rules as .nephilex.yml (see Which configuration is trusted). A sanitizer entry switches checks off, so the file must never come from the code it is meant to review.

Situation .nephilex/context.yml Local path (nephilex scan .) Honoured Cloned remote (nephilex scan https://...) Ignored unless --trust-remote-config --config-from-ref REF Read from that git ref; the working tree's copy is ignored nephilex agent, nephilex mcp Ignored

In CI on pull requests, use --config-from-ref origin/<base-branch> (the GitHub Action does this by default). A pull request that adds or edits .nephilex/context.yml then has no effect on its own scan: the version already reviewed and merged on the base branch decides. Changes to the context file take effect after they are merged, like any other gate setting.

Treat changes to .nephilex/context.yml like changes to the gate itself: put the file under CODEOWNERS for your security reviewers.

docs.title: Schema
docs.text:
All sections are optional. Unknown keys, wrong types, unknown languages, CWE ids that do not look like CWE-79, and names that are not dotted identifiers are configuration errors: the run stops with exit status 2 instead of scanning with a setting that does not say what you meant.

version: 1                      # optional; 1 is the only version

sanitizers:
  python:                       # python | javascript | typescript (alias of javascript)
    - myapp.db.quote_identifier # a bare name clears taint for every sink
    - name: myapp.security.escape_html
      cwe: [CWE-79]             # only for sinks of these CWEs
      note: wraps markupsafe.escape
  javascript:
    - name: lib.html.htmlSafe
      cwe: CWE-79               # a single CWE may be a string

trusted_sources:
  python:
    - os.environ                # deploy-time configuration, not user input
    - name: myapp.settings.get
      note: reads the service's own config file
  javascript:
    - process.env

internal_paths:
  - scripts/**
  - path: migrations/*.py
    note: run by operators during deploys

exposure:
  - path: api/**
    level: public_api           # public_api | public_web | internal_service | offline
  - path: worker/**
    level: internal_service
    note: consumes an internal queue only

data_classification:
  - path: billing/**
    classes: [financial, pii]   # pii | secrets | credentials | financial | health
  - model: myapp.models.Customer
    classes: [pii]

Limits: at most 1000 entries per section, names up to 200 characters, notes up to 500 characters, and the file itself up to 1 MB.

docs.title: sanitizers
docs.text:
A call matches a configured sanitizer when the dotted name at the call site is a trailing part of the configured name. For myapp.security.escape_html:

Call Matches escape_html(x) yes security.escape_html(x) yes myapp.security.escape_html(x) yes other.escape_html(x) no self.escape_html(x) no

Imports are not resolved, so a different function with the same short name also matches a bare call. Prefer distinctive names, and configure the name the way your code calls it.

With cwe, the sanitizer only clears taint for sinks of those CWEs. The value stays tainted for every other sink, through any number of assignments:

from myapp.security import safe_path


def download():
    p = safe_path(request.args["file"])  # sanitizer for CWE-22 only
    q = p
    send_file(q)  # not reported: path traversal is handled
    os.system("gzip " + q)  # still reported: command injection

The CWEs the taint tiers check are CWE-89 (SQL injection), CWE-78 (command injection), CWE-22 (path traversal), CWE-95 (code injection) and, for JavaScript, CWE-79 (cross-site scripting).

JavaScript example:

sanitizers:
  javascript:
    - name: lib.html.htmlSafe
      cwe: [CWE-79]

const name = html.htmlSafe(req.query.name);
el.innerHTML = name;                              // not reported
db.query("SELECT * FROM t WHERE n = '" + name + "'");  // still reported (CWE-89)

docs.title: trusted_sources
docs.text:
Each entry is a dotted name. A call to it (matched like a sanitizer) yields a clean value whatever its arguments, and the name itself no longer counts as an input source where Nephilex treats it as one by default (os.environ and sys.argv in Python, process.env and process.argv in JavaScript):

table = os.environ.get("REPORT_TABLE")  # with trusted_sources: [os.environ]
cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM " + table)  # not reported

Only list values an attacker cannot influence in your deployment. Environment variables are a good fit for a server; they are not for a CLI tool that other users run with their own environment.

docs.title: internal_paths
docs.text:
Path globs, matched against the project-relative path like allowlist paths: * crosses directories, dir/** matches everything below dir/, and a glob without / also matches the file name anywhere. Each finding under a matching path is lowered one severity level (High becomes Medium, Info stays Info) and tagged internal.

The finding is never removed. min_severity is applied to the severity before the downgrade, so --min-severity high still shows a High finding that the context lowered to Medium. --fail-on uses the lowered severity, which is the point: an internal-only High no longer fails a fail_on: high gate, but it is still in the report.

docs.title: exposure
docs.text: public_api and public_web raise likelihood one step (for example Possible to Likely); internal_service and offline lower it one step. Likelihood feeds the risk score and ranking, not the severity gate. The first matching entry wins.

docs.title: data_classification
docs.text: Each entry needs a path glob, a model name, or both, and a non-empty list of classes. A finding of severity Low or above under the path, or whose code snippet mentions the model's short name as a whole word (Customer, not Customers), is raised one severity level and tagged sensitive-data plus each class. The first matching entry wins. When a finding is both in sensitive data and in an internal path, both changes apply and both are recorded.

docs.title: Reviewing what the context changed
docs.text:
A finding the context changed carries the original values and one entry per setting that applied:

"metadata": {
  "context": {
    "source": ".nephilex/context.yml",
    "original_severity": "high",
    "original_likelihood": "possible",
    "changes": [
      {
        "setting": "internal_paths",
        "match": "scripts/**",
        "effect": "severity high -> medium",
        "why": "run by operators during deploys"
      }
    ]
  }
}

Flows cleared by a sanitizer or trusted source are not findings any more, so they are listed in the report's project_summary.context.cleared, with the rule, path, line and the context entries that occur in the file:

"context": {
  "source": "origin/main:.nephilex/context.yml",
  "digest": "3f2a9c0d1e4b5a67",
  "internal": 1,
  "exposure": 0,
  "sensitive_data": 0,
  "cleared": [
    {
      "rule": "ast-python.ast-path-traversal",
      "path": "app/download.py",
      "line": 7,
      "entries": ["myapp.security.safe_path"],
      "why": "a sanitizer or trusted source declared in the project context removes the taint on this flow"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Sanitizers and trusted sources apply to the intra-file AST taint tiers (ast-python, ast-js). The regex patterns tier and the cross-file Python tier do not read them. Where an AST tier analysed a file, the regex tier's findings for SQL injection, XSS, path traversal and code injection are already dropped in favour of the AST result, so the sanitizer still takes effect for those classes.
  • Matching is by name, not by resolved import or type.
  • Editing the context file invalidates the scan cache for the taint tiers, so a warm scan picks up the change.

docs.title: Web dashboard
docs.text:
The dashboard is an optional local web app for teams who want scan history and trends instead of one-off CLI reports. It stores every scan you send it in a small SQLite database and shows projects, risk over time, and findings.

For Nephilex Cloud (hosted) and how users interpret risk scores and drift, see Understanding scan results.

It never runs by default and the base nephilex install stays lightweight, the dashboard and its dependencies live behind the dashboard extra.

docs.title: Install & run
docs.text:
pip install "nephilex[dashboard]"
nephilex dashboard            # serves http://127.0.0.1:8000

Options: --host (default 127.0.0.1) and --port (default 8000).

The database lives at ~/.nephilex/dashboard.db by default; override with the NEPHILEX_DASHBOARD_DB environment variable. On Linux and macOS the database is created readable by your user only.

docs.title: Access and security
docs.text:
The dashboard holds code snippets and a list of your vulnerabilities, so it is locked down by default:

  • It binds to 127.0.0.1 and only answers requests whose Host header is a loopback name, which blocks DNS-rebinding attacks from web pages you visit. Add further names with NEPHILEX_DASHBOARD_ALLOWED_HOSTS (comma-separated).
  • Binding to any other address requires a token. Set NEPHILEX_DASHBOARD_TOKEN and the dashboard accepts it as a bearer token, or once through a login link (http://HOST:PORT/?token=...). Without a token, a non-loopback --host is refused with exit code 2. Serve it behind TLS when it leaves your machine.
  • Uploads and the API reject cross-site requests, and every page is sent with a restrictive Content Security Policy.
  • Only the newest NEPHILEX_DASHBOARD_MAX_SCANS scans are kept (default 1000).
export NEPHILEX_DASHBOARD_TOKEN="$(python -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))')"
nephilex dashboard --host 0.0.0.0 --port 9000

docs.title: Getting scans in
docs.text:
The dashboard reads Nephilex's normal JSON report, there are two ways to send one.

Upload in the browser:

nephilex scan . -f json -o report.json
# then open http://127.0.0.1:8000/upload and pick report.json

Pipe it straight from the CLI (great for CI):

nephilex scan . -f json | curl -s -X POST --data-binary @- \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/scans

The Content-Type header is required; other content types are rejected with HTTP 415. Add -H "Authorization: Bearer $NEPHILEX_DASHBOARD_TOKEN" when a token is set.

Each scan is grouped into a project by name, so scanning the same project over time builds its history and trend automatically.

docs.title: What you see
docs.text:
• Projects, every project with its latest risk score, severity mix, and when it was last scanned; worst risk first.
  • Project detail, a risk-over-time line chart and the full scan history.
  • Scan detail, the aggregate risk, a severity breakdown, and a filterable / searchable list of findings, each expandable to its reasoning and remediation.

docs.title: Design & data handling
docs.text:
• No re-computation. Ingestion parses the report back into Nephilex's own ScanResult, so the dashboard's risk scores and severity counts are computed by the same code as the CLI and can never disagree with it.
  • Local and private. It's a local app over SQLite, your findings stay on your machine. It has no authentication, so run it locally or behind your own access control; don't expose it to the public internet as-is.
  • Colors come from a validated, colorblind-safe palette, and severity is always shown with its label, never by color alone.

docs.title: Configuration drift
docs.text: Compare two point-in-time snapshots to see what changed in security posture or project composition.

docs.title: Scan drift
docs.text:
Save two Nephilex JSON reports, then diff them:

nephilex scan . -f json -o baseline.json
# ... changes land in the repo ...
nephilex scan . -f json -o current.json
nephilex drift baseline.json current.json
nephilex drift baseline.json current.json --fail-on high -o drift.json

Drift uses stable finding fingerprints (rule + path + snippet hash), so line number shifts alone do not look like new vulnerabilities.

Output categories:

  • added - new findings since the baseline
  • removed - findings that disappeared (fixed or no longer detected)
  • severity_changed - same finding, higher or lower severity

docs.title: Inventory drift
docs.text:
Compare two nephilex inventory exports for dependency and architecture changes:

nephilex inventory . -o inv-before.json
nephilex inventory . -o inv-after.json
nephilex drift inv-before.json inv-after.json --inventory

Reports:

  • dependency adds, removes, and version changes
  • new or removed CI/CD, container, and IaC files

docs.title: CI usage
docs.text:
Gate deployments on posture regressions:

- run: nephilex scan . -f json -o current.json
- run: nephilex drift baseline.json current.json --fail-on high --quiet

Store baseline.json from the last known-good release tag or scheduled scan.

docs.title: Continuous monitoring (nephilex watch)
docs.text:
Run periodic scans locally, keep snapshots under .nephilex/watch/, and detect drift between cycles:

nephilex watch . --interval 300          # scan every 5 minutes
nephilex watch . --once                  # single cycle (cron-friendly)
nephilex watch . --push                  # upload each scan to Nephilex Cloud
nephilex watch . --fail-on-drift high    # exit non-zero on new High+ findings

Pair with nephilex push and the Nephilex Cloud dashboard for hosted history and scan-to-scan drift in the UI.

docs.title: Server agent (nephilex agent)
docs.text:
For hosts that monitor multiple paths, use the server agent with a config file:

nephilex agent --init
nephilex agent --once

See agent.md for systemd and cron deployment examples.

docs.title: Editors and AI assistants
docs.text:
Nephilex can check code while it is being written, by you or by an AI coding assistant. There are two pieces, and most setups use both:

  • A hook or task runs nephilex check on a file right after it is edited. It is fast, offline and needs no cooperation from the model.
  • The MCP server (nephilex mcp) gives the assistant tools it can call itself: check files or a snippet, check a dependency before adding it, and get a verified fix as a diff. See MCP server for the tool reference.

nephilex init --editor claude|cursor|vscode writes the project config for both. It never overwrites an existing file unless you pass --force, and with --force it merges the Nephilex entries into existing JSON files, keeping your other settings.

docs.title: nephilex check
docs.text:
nephilex check src/app.py                 # human-readable
nephilex check src/app.py -f json         # same schema as `nephilex scan -f json`
nephilex check src/app.py -f hook         # one line per finding
nephilex check a.py b.ts --fail-on critical

nephilex check scans only the files you name, with only the file-local scanners: secrets, the SAST patterns, the AST taint tiers (Python, JavaScript/TypeScript), IaC, LLM/AI usage, malware, and the other built-in scanners whose findings depend on a single file (CI workflows, Dockerfiles, cloud config, language rules). Dependency, OSV and cross-file analyses are left to nephilex scan.

  • It reuses the scan cache, so an unchanged file costs almost nothing. It does not prune cache entries for other files, so it never slows down the next full scan.
  • It makes no network calls: secret verification and git-history scanning are always off for a check, whatever .nephilex.yml says.
  • It does no AI enrichment unless you pass --ai.
  • It reads .nephilex.yml from the project root like nephilex scan, including exclude_paths, scanners, exclude_scanners and allow entries.

The project root is the nearest directory at or above the current one that holds .git or .nephilex.yml (or --root). A path outside it, a missing file or a directory is refused with exit status 2. Files inside directories Nephilex never scans (node_modules, .git, dist, ...) and files matching exclude_paths are skipped with a note on stderr.

Exit status: 0 when nothing is at or above --fail-on (default high), 1 when something is or a scanner crashed (set fail_on_error: false to ignore crashes), 2 for usage errors.

docs.title: Strict mode for AI assistants
docs.text:
An inline nephilex-ignore comment hides a finding on its line, which is what a developer wants after reviewing it. An AI assistant that is told about a finding can add the same comment to make the hook go quiet instead of fixing the code. --no-inline-ignores ignores those comments for the run, so every finding in the file is reported whatever comments it carries:

nephilex check src/app.py --no-inline-ignores

The hooks that nephilex init --editor claude and nephilex init --editor cursor write use it. Suppressions kept outside the source (allow: entries in .nephilex.yml and .nephilex/exceptions.yml) still apply, and a full nephilex scan still honours inline comments, so a comment a reviewer accepted keeps working in CI. Put those files under CODEOWNERS if an assistant must not change them either.

docs.title: The hook format
docs.text:
src/app.py:12:5: error high patterns.python-yaml-load: Unsafe yaml.load without SafeLoader. Fix: Use yaml.safe_load, or yaml.load(..., Loader=yaml.SafeLoader).

That is path:line:column: level severity rule-id: title. Fix: hint. The path is relative to the project root. level is error for critical and high, warning for medium and info for low and info, so an editor problem matcher can use it. Clean files print nothing.

docs.title: Editor hook mode
docs.text: nephilex check --hook claude and nephilex check --hook cursor read the hook event the editor writes to stdin, check the edited file, and answer in that editor's hook protocol. Writes outside the project and deleted files are ignored silently (exit 0). Problems with Nephilex itself, such as an invalid config, exit 1, which both editors treat as a non-blocking hook error.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text: Measured on Windows 11 with Python 3.11, checking one 300-line Python file: the check itself takes about 75 ms with a warm cache and about 220 ms without one. The whole nephilex check process takes about 0.7 to 0.9 s, most of it Python startup and importing Nephilex; under heavy load it is slower. nephilex check does not import the report formats, the AI provider clients or their HTTP library unless it needs them (-f json loads the JSON reporter, --ai the provider).

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
nephilex init --editor claude

This writes two files.

.mcp.json registers the MCP server for the project:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "nephilex": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "nephilex",
      "args": ["mcp"],
      "env": {}
    }
  }
}

.claude/settings.json adds a PostToolUse hook that runs after the Edit and Write tools:

{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "nephilex check --hook claude --no-inline-ignores",
            "timeout": 30
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

The hook reads tool_input.file_path from the event. When the file has findings at or above --fail-on (default high), it answers with {"decision": "block", "reason": "..."}: the edit has already happened, and Claude Code shows the reason, one hook-format line per finding, to Claude next to the tool result so it fixes the code. Lower findings are passed as additionalContext instead. A clean file produces no output. --no-inline-ignores makes the hook report findings even where Claude added a nephilex-ignore comment (see Strict mode).

To gate on a different severity, edit the command, for example nephilex check --hook claude --no-inline-ignores --fail-on medium.

Claude Code asks you to approve a project MCP server from .mcp.json the first time; approve nephilex.

docs.title: Verify in 5 minutes
docs.text:
1. Run nephilex --version in the project directory. If it fails, the hook and server cannot start either; see Troubleshooting.
  2. Start Claude Code in the project and approve the nephilex server. Run /mcp and check that nephilex is connected with five tools.
  3. Run /hooks and check that a PostToolUse hook with matcher Edit|Write runs nephilex check --hook claude --no-inline-ignores.
  4. Ask: "Create demo_nephilex.py with a function that loads YAML using yaml.load". After the write, Claude should mention the Nephilex finding (patterns.python-yaml-load) and switch to yaml.safe_load on its own.
  5. Ask: "Call nephilex_check_files on demo_nephilex.py, then nephilex_fix on the finding". It should get a diff back and say it was not applied.
  6. Ask: "Use nephilex_check_package to check the npm package lodahs". The verdict should be suspicious (it resembles lodash).
  7. Delete demo_nephilex.py.

docs.title: Cursor
docs.text:
nephilex init --editor cursor

This writes three files.

.cursor/mcp.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "nephilex": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "nephilex",
      "args": ["mcp"],
      "env": {"NEPHILEX_MCP_ROOTS": "${workspaceFolder}"}
    }
  }
}

NEPHILEX_MCP_ROOTS pins the project root, because Cursor's documentation does not say which directory it starts the server in.

.cursor/hooks.json:

{
  "version": 1,
  "hooks": {
    "afterFileEdit": [
      {"command": "nephilex check --hook cursor --no-inline-ignores", "timeout": 30}
    ]
  }
}

Cursor's afterFileEdit hook has no output the agent reads, so the hook writes its findings to stderr (Cursor's Hooks output channel is the documented place to debug hooks; its documentation does not say whether hook stderr is shown there), and the agent is told to use the MCP tools by a project rule:

.cursor/rules/nephilex.mdc is an Always Apply rule that tells the agent to call nephilex_check_files after it writes code, nephilex_check_package before adding a dependency, nephilex_fix for verified fixes, and not to silence findings with nephilex-ignore comments. Edit it to suit your team.

docs.title: Verify in 5 minutes
docs.text:
1. Run nephilex --version in the project directory.
  2. Open the project in Cursor. In Cursor Settings, under MCP, check that the nephilex server is enabled and lists five tools.
  3. In Cursor Settings, under Rules, check that nephilex is listed as a project rule that always applies.
  4. In the Agent, ask: "Create demo_nephilex.py with a function that loads YAML using yaml.load". The agent should call nephilex_check_files afterwards (shown as a tool call) and fix the finding.
  5. Open the Output panel, choose the Hooks channel, and check that the afterFileEdit hook ran without errors. If your Cursor version shows hook stderr there, the patterns.python-yaml-load line appears too.
  6. Ask the agent to check the npm package lodahs with Nephilex; the verdict should be suspicious.
  7. Delete demo_nephilex.py.

docs.title: VS Code
docs.text:
nephilex init --editor vscode

This writes two files.

.vscode/mcp.json (VS Code uses a top-level servers key):

{
  "servers": {
    "nephilex": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "nephilex",
      "args": ["mcp"],
      "cwd": "${workspaceFolder}"
    }
  }
}

.vscode/tasks.json adds a "Nephilex: check current file" task that runs nephilex check --format hook on the active file. Its problem matcher turns each finding into an entry in the Problems panel:

{
  "version": "2.0.0",
  "tasks": [
    {
      "label": "Nephilex: check current file",
      "type": "process",
      "command": "nephilex",
      "args": ["check", "--root", "${workspaceFolder}", "--format", "hook", "${file}"],
      "problemMatcher": {
        "owner": "nephilex",
        "source": "nephilex",
        "fileLocation": ["relative", "${workspaceFolder}"],
        "pattern": {
          "regexp": "^(.+?):(\\d+):(\\d+): (error|warning|info) (\\S+) (\\S+): (.*)$",
          "file": 1,
          "line": 2,
          "column": 3,
          "severity": 4,
          "code": 6,
          "message": 7
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

The task exits 1 when it finds something at or above high, so VS Code reports the task as failed; the findings are in the Problems panel either way.

nephilex init cannot merge into a tasks.json that contains comments (VS Code allows them). In that case it stops without writing anything; copy the task above into your file by hand.

docs.title: Verify in 5 minutes
docs.text:
1. Run nephilex --version in the integrated terminal.
  2. Open .vscode/mcp.json; VS Code shows a Start action above the nephilex server. Start it and check that it reports five tools.
  3. In the Chat view, switch to Agent mode, open the tools picker and check that the nephilex tools are listed.
  4. Create demo_nephilex.py containing import yaml and data = yaml.load(open("x")). Run Terminal, Run Task, "Nephilex: check current file". The Problems panel should show an error on line 2 with code patterns.python-yaml-load.
  5. In Agent mode, ask: "Call nephilex_check_files on demo_nephilex.py, then nephilex_fix on the finding". Approve the tool calls; the reply should include a diff that was not applied.
  6. Delete demo_nephilex.py.

docs.title: Other MCP clients
docs.text:
Windsurf, Cline, Continue, Zed, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI and other MCP clients can run Nephilex as a stdio server. Their config file formats differ and Nephilex has not verified them, so register it through the client's own MCP settings with:

  • command: nephilex
  • arguments: mcp
  • transport: stdio
  • optional environment: NEPHILEX_MCP_ROOTS=<your project directory> if the client does not start servers in the project directory.

Many clients accept the common mcpServers shape:

{"mcpServers": {"nephilex": {"command": "nephilex", "args": ["mcp"]}}}

docs.title: Verify in 5 minutes
docs.text:
1. Run nephilex --version in the project directory.
  2. Register the server as above and restart the client.
  3. Check that the client lists the five nephilex_* tools.
  4. Ask the assistant to call nephilex_check_snippet with import yaml\nyaml.load(s) and language python. It should report patterns.python-yaml-load on line 2.
  5. Ask it to call nephilex_fix with that finding's id; it should return a diff using yaml.safe_load and say it was not applied.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• nephilex is not found by the editor. Editors started from a desktop launcher may not see the shell PATH of a virtual environment. Use the absolute path to the nephilex executable (for example /path/to/venv/bin/nephilex or C:\path\to\venv\Scripts\nephilex.exe) as the command in the generated files.
  • The MCP tools refuse a path as outside the allowed roots. The server only reads files under the directory it was started in, or under NEPHILEX_MCP_ROOTS. Set NEPHILEX_MCP_ROOTS to the project directory in the server's env.
  • No network. Set NEPHILEX_MCP_OFFLINE=1 in the server's env to keep nephilex_check_package offline. The other tools never use the network.

docs.title: Formats verified
docs.text:
Editor config formats change. Each generated file was checked against the official documentation on 2026-10-22; the template source in src/nephilex/integrations/editors.py records the same pages.

File Documentation .mcp.json https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp .claude/settings.json hooks https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks .cursor/mcp.json https://cursor.com/docs/context/mcp .cursor/hooks.json https://cursor.com/docs/agent/hooks .cursor/rules/nephilex.mdc https://cursor.com/docs/context/rules .vscode/mcp.json https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/reference/mcp-configuration .vscode/tasks.json https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/debugtest/tasks

docs.title: Why was this reported? Evidence and grades
docs.text:
Every finding carries an evidence block. It answers two questions: why Nephilex reported the finding, and how you can check it yourself by reading the code.

Evidence explains a finding. It does not change what is detected: the same findings, with the same rule, location, severity, confidence and fingerprint, are reported with or without it.

docs.title: What the evidence block contains
docs.text:
Field What it holds grade confirmed, likely or possible: what kind of proof backs the finding (table below). basis One sentence saying what the grade rests on, for example "Request data reaches the SQL call with no recognized sanitizer on the path." path The lines from where the data comes from to where it is used, in order. Each step has path (file), line, column (when known), role, code (that source line) and a short note. verify Two to four plain steps to confirm or rule out the finding by reading the code.

A step's role is one of:

  • source: where the data comes from (request.args['q'], req.query.q).
  • step: an assignment, a call into a helper, or a parameter that receives the value.
  • guard: a check Nephilex saw on the way that does not cover this kind of sink (for example a path containment check before an SQL call).
  • sink: where the value is used (cursor.execute, child_process.exec()).
  • elided: a marker where steps were left out of a long path.

docs.title: Grades
docs.text:
The rules live in one place, src/nephilex/core/evidence.py. They are conservative: when a rule does not clearly apply, the weaker grade wins.

Grade Meaning When Nephilex assigns it confirmed Proved without guessing. A secret in a provider's exact key format that the provider accepted as live (only with secret validation on). A dependency whose exact installed version, from a lock file or an == pin in requirements.txt, is inside an advisory's affected range. A finding that an active check (the dynamic scan, a container image inspection, file integrity monitoring) marked verified or confirmed. likely Traced, or an exact match. Taint data flow from an attacker-controlled source (request data, browser input, an archive entry name) to the sink with no recognized sanitizer on the recorded path, at medium or high confidence. A finding that took over such a path because two scanners reported the same weakness (see below). A high-confidence rule of a precise scanner (patterns, lang-sast, secrets, iac, cicd, agent-config, container, cloud) that matched the exact code. A dependency version required in go.mod. possible Worth reading; not shown to be reachable by an attacker. Everything else: heuristic and pattern matches, low confidence, operator input (command line, environment, console), library-mode findings (public-api), test and example code, results imported from another tool's SARIF, dependency versions taken from a range (package.json), and data-flow findings whose source was not recorded.

Checks that make a finding possible (test code, operator input, library mode, low confidence) come before likely, so a traced flow inside a test file is still possible. confirmed comes first: a live credential is live wherever it sits.

The grade is separate from confidence. Confidence is each scanner's own estimate and feeds sorting and risk scores; the grade only says what kind of proof is behind the finding. Neither --fail-on nor any other gate reads the grade. A possible finding is not a false positive: it is one Nephilex could not back with a traced flow or a check.

docs.title: Where the path comes from
docs.text:
• Python (ast-python): the taint engine records where a value became tainted, each assignment it went through, same-file helpers that returned it, checks that did not cover the sink, and the sink.
  • Python across files (ast-python-xfile): the source at the call site, the call, the parameter that receives the value in the other file, the steps inside that function, and the sink there.
  • JavaScript and TypeScript (ast-js): the source, assignments, calls into same-file helpers and the sink. For a flow that goes through a helper, the finding is shown at the call and the path ends at the sink inside the helper.
  • Every other scanner (patterns, secrets, dependencies, IaC, CI/CD, agent configuration, authorization, malware and the rest): one step, the matched line, with verification steps written for that kind of finding.

When two scanners report the same weakness a few lines apart, Nephilex keeps one finding (for example the pattern finding, because it has a deterministic fix). If the kept finding has no path of its own and the other one traced attacker-controlled data to the sink, the kept finding shows that path.

A path shows one route the value took. When several routes reach the same sink, the engine keeps the first it recorded, preferring one that starts at request data. Paths are capped at 12 steps: the source, an elided marker, and the steps closest to the sink.

docs.title: Example: one SQL injection in every format
docs.text:
The code, app.py:

import sqlite3
from flask import Flask, request
app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route('/search')
def search():
    q = request.args['q']
    query = "SELECT * FROM items WHERE name = '" + q + "'"
    cursor = sqlite3.connect('db').cursor()
    cursor.execute(query)
    return 'ok'

Everything below was produced by scanning a folder holding only this file with --no-ai. Outputs are pasted as printed, trimmed only where marked.

<details><summary>Evidence: likely</summary>

docs.title: MCP
docs.text: The nephilex_scan tool of the MCP server returns the same block for each finding as evidence, with grade, basis, path (each step's path, line, role, code and note) and verify.

docs.title: How to use verify
docs.text:
The verify steps are a short review checklist, written so you can settle a finding without running anything:

  1. Open the source line and confirm the value really comes from where the note says (a request parameter, a browser URL, an archive entry).
  2. Follow the listed lines and look for anything that validates, escapes or converts the value before the sink. Nephilex recognizes common sanitizers and checks; a project-specific one it does not know shows up here.
  3. Check callers, decorators and middleware for validation that happens before the code shown.
  4. Where a step suggests trying an input, do it only in a test environment you own. Nephilex never suggests testing a system you do not own.

If you confirm the finding, fix it. If you rule it out, record why: an inline nephilex-ignore comment, an entry in .nephilex/exceptions.yml, or a baseline (see Triage & baselines).

docs.title: Code from the scanned repository
docs.text: The code and note of each step quote the scanned repository, which may be hostile. Before they are stored, they are reduced to one line, cut to a fixed length, control, bidirectional and zero-width characters are shown as <U+XXXX>, and secret-looking values are masked, the same way finding snippets from instruction files are made safe. Each report format escapes them again for its own syntax (HTML escaping, Markdown code spans, Rich markup escaping in the terminal). Nephilex never runs this text or puts it in a shell command.

docs.title: Example finding: unsafe yaml.load
docs.text:
This page follows one real finding from the demo app in examples/vulnerable-app from the vulnerable line to a committed fix and a re-scan. It was chosen because the untrusted input and the dangerous call are both visible, Nephilex uses data flow to grade it, and Nephilex has a deterministic fix for it.

Everything below was produced by Nephilex 0.11.0 on 2026-10-23 with --no-ai (no AI provider, no API key). The commands are the ones from the Quickstart; outputs are pasted as printed, trimmed only where marked.

docs.title: The vulnerable code
docs.text:
examples/vulnerable-app/app.py, lines 41 to 45:

@app.route("/config")
def load_config():
    # Unsafe deserialization (patterns scanner: CWE-502).
    raw = request.args.get("data")
    return str(yaml.load(raw))

Line 44 reads the data query parameter, which anyone who can reach /config controls. Line 45 passes it to yaml.load without a safe loader, which can build arbitrary Python objects from the document.

docs.title: How Nephilex reports it
docs.text:
The row in the terminal table of nephilex scan nephilex/examples/vulnerable-app --no-ai (trimmed to this one row):

│ High     │ 70.5 │ Unsafe yaml.load without          │ app.py:45        │ patterns.python-yaml-load        │
│          │      │ SafeLoader                        │                  │                                  │

The same finding in the Markdown report (nephilex scan nephilex/examples/vulnerable-app --no-ai --patches -f json -f markdown -o ex, file ex/nephilex-report.md, finding 6 of 20):

### 6. [HIGH] Unsafe yaml.load without SafeLoader

- **Severity:** High (risk 70.5/100), **Confidence:** High, **Likelihood:** Possible
- **Location:** `app.py:45`
- **Scanner/Rule:** `patterns` / `patterns.python-yaml-load`
- **Mapping:** CWE-502, A08:2021-Software and Data Integrity Failures

```
    return str(yaml.load(raw))
```

**Why it's a vulnerability:** yaml.load with the default loader can construct arbitrary Python objects from the document.

**How an attacker exploits it:** Feed a YAML payload using \`\!\!python/object/apply\` tags to execute code.

**Business impact:** Remote code execution.

**Remediation:** Use yaml.safe\_load, or yaml.load\(..., Loader=yaml.SafeLoader\).

**Suggested patch (verified):**
```diff
--- a/app.py
+++ b/app.py
@@ -45 +45 @@
-    return str(yaml.load(raw))
+    return str(yaml.safe_load(raw))
```

docs.title: Reading the fields
docs.text:
Field Value Where it comes from Rule patterns.python-yaml-load A rule in the patterns scanner, which matches source lines; see SAST (pattern rules). Severity High (3) The rule's severity: an unsafe YAML loader on input can lead to code execution. Confidence High (2) Raised from the rule's default because the data-flow engine found that the argument comes from request data ("dataflow": "tainted"). Likelihood Possible (2) The pattern scanner's default. CWE / OWASP CWE-502, A08:2021 Deserialization of untrusted data; Software and Data Integrity Failures. Risk 70.5, contextual 80.5 The risk score combines severity, confidence and likelihood; the contextual score adds 10 because the severity is High or above. See Risk score.

The JSON stores severity, confidence and likelihood as numbers: severity runs from 0 (Info) to 4 (Critical), confidence from 0 (Low) to 2 (High), likelihood from 0 (Rare) to 4 (Almost certain).

The confidence grade depends on the [ast] extra. The same scan with a plain pip install nephilex (no tree-sitter) reports this finding with confidence Medium (1), no dataflow key, and risk 64.2.

docs.title: Source to sink
docs.text:
Nephilex does not print a step-by-step path for this finding. What it records is the data-flow verdict for the call on line 45, "dataflow": "tainted": the argument to yaml.load was traced back to request data. The source (line 44, request.args.get) and the sink (line 45, yaml.load) above are read from the code, not from the report.

Versions after 0.11.0 do record this path: every finding has an evidence block with a grade, the steps from source to sink and how to verify it. For this finding the path is request.args.get("data") (line 44), assigned to raw (line 44), passed to yaml.load (line 45), graded likely. See Evidence and grades.

Two other results point at the same line:

  • The taint scanner reports ast-python.ast-xss on line 45 (Medium): the parsed request data is returned from a Flask view as the response body.
  • The taint scanner also traces the request data into yaml.load on this line. Both tiers report the same weakness, so Nephilex keeps one finding: the pattern finding, because it carries the deterministic fix. nephilex scan and nephilex check make the same choice.
